rd-school-c7-science-a.ch02-nutrition-in.title: Nutrition in Animals
rd-school-c7-science-a.ch02-nutrition-in.subtitle: The nine-metre journey of a samosa through your body

sections.md:
You bite into a hot samosa. Within hours, the potato inside has become energy for your cricket match and material for your growing bones. But how does a lump of potato become *you*? It must be broken into tiny, soluble pieces that blood can carry. That breaking-down is **digestion**.

Plants make their own food by photosynthesis. Animals cannot — they depend directly or indirectly on plants. A goat eats grass; a tiger eats the goat. So all animals are **heterotrophs**. **Animal nutrition** includes the need for nutrients, the mode of intake of food and how the body uses it.

Food contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. Carbohydrates like starch are *complex* — the body cannot use them as they are. They must be broken down into *simple* substances. The whole process has five steps:
1. **Ingestion** — taking food into the body.
2. **Digestion** — breaking complex food into simple soluble substances.
3. **Absorption** — digested food passing into blood.
4. **Assimilation** — using absorbed food to make new body material and energy.
5. **Egestion** — removing undigested waste.

check.q: Converting complex food into simpler soluble substances is called:
check.why: Digestion is the breaking down of complex food components into simple, soluble forms the body can absorb.

sections.md:
The way food is taken in differs from animal to animal, and it depends on what the animal eats. Look around you — at home, in a garden, near a pond:

- A **snake** (and a frog) swallows its prey whole.
- A **mosquito** pierces skin and **sucks** blood with a needle-like mouth.
- A **housefly** sponges up liquid food.
- A **butterfly** and a **hummingbird** sip flower **nectar**.
- An **eagle** tears flesh with a hooked beak; a **lion** with sharp canines.
- An **ant** and a **cockroach** chew with mouthparts; a **cow** scrapes and chews grass.
- A **honeybee** sucks nectar; a **lice** sucks blood from the scalp.
- An **ant-eater** flicks out a long sticky tongue.

The most surprising feeder is the **starfish**. It eats animals with hard shells such as clams and oysters. It opens the shell, then pushes out its stomach through its mouth, digests the soft animal inside the shell, and pulls its stomach back in — leaving the empty shell behind.

head: Animal
Kind of food
Mode of feeding
fig.caption: Many animals, many ways to eat.

check.q: Which animal pushes its stomach out of its mouth to feed?
check.why: A starfish everts its stomach through its mouth to digest the soft body of a clam inside its shell.

sections.md:
In humans, food travels through a continuous tube about 9 metres long called the **alimentary canal**, from the mouth to the anus. Its parts are:

**Buccal cavity (mouth) → Oesophagus (food pipe) → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine → Rectum → Anus**

Glands along the way — **salivary glands, liver, pancreas** — pour in digestive juices. The inner wall of the stomach and small intestine also secrete juices. The canal and its glands together form the **digestive system**.

You can feel parts of it yourself. Put your hand on the upper left of your belly after a meal — that is near the stomach. The liver sits on the upper right, partly under the ribs.

check.why: Food passes from mouth to oesophagus to stomach and then into the small intestine.

sections.h: The mouth and buccal cavity: teeth
sections.md:
Food is ingested through the mouth, into the **buccal cavity**. Digestion starts here. **Teeth** cut and grind food into small pieces (mechanical digestion). Each tooth sits in a separate socket in the gums.

Try this activity: wash your hands, then feel your teeth with a finger, or look in a mirror. You will find teeth of different shapes:

| Teeth | Number (adult) | Shape | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incisors | 8 | Flat, chisel-like, in front | Cutting and biting |
| Canines | 4 | Pointed | Piercing and tearing |
| Premolars | 8 | Broad with ridges | Chewing and grinding |
| Molars | 12 | Broadest, at the back | Chewing and grinding |

That's 32 teeth in an adult (16 in each jaw). Our first set, **milk teeth**, grows in infancy and falls out between ages 6 and 8. **Permanent teeth** replace them and last a lifetime — or until lost through disease or accident. Look at a younger sibling: a gap in front is a milk tooth that just fell out!

check.q: Which teeth are used for tearing food?
check.why: Canines are pointed teeth suited for piercing and tearing food.

sections.h: Saliva, the tongue, and tooth decay
sections.md:
Our mouth has **salivary glands** that secrete **saliva**. Saliva wets the food and contains an enzyme that breaks down **starch into sugar**.

**Activity (from the chapter's idea):** Take two test tubes with a little boiled rice. Add a few drops of saliva to one and nothing to the other. After 30–40 minutes add a drop of iodine solution to both. The tube without saliva turns **blue-black** (starch still present). The tube with saliva shows little or no colour change — the starch has been digested. Chew a piece of roti for a minute and you will taste the sweetness yourself.

The **tongue** is a fleshy muscular organ attached at the back to the floor of the mouth. It is free at the front. We use it for talking, mixing food with saliva and pushing food down for swallowing. It carries **taste buds** that detect sweet, salty, sour and bitter tastes.

**Tooth decay.** Bacteria always live in our mouth. Most are harmless, but if we do not clean teeth after eating, harmful bacteria grow on leftover sugars and release **acids**. The acids slowly damage the hard enamel. This causes **tooth decay**; if not treated, it leads to toothache and even loss of the tooth. Chocolates, sweets, cold drinks and sugary foods are major culprits.

Prevention: brush twice a day, use dental floss, rinse after every meal, avoid putting dirty fingers or unwashed objects in the mouth, and limit sweets.

check.q: In the saliva activity, which tube turns blue-black with iodine?
check.why: Iodine turns blue-black only where starch remains, and starch remains in the tube where saliva did not digest it.

sections.md:
Swallowed food goes down the **oesophagus**, a muscular tube running through the neck and chest. Its walls contract and relax in waves that push food down — in fact, such movements happen along the whole canal. Sometimes, when you eat in a hurry or talk while eating, food enters the windpipe instead; you cough and feel a choke. A flap called the **epiglottis** normally closes the windpipe during swallowing.

Sometimes food is not accepted by the stomach and is vomited out — think of a time you felt sick after a bad meal.

The **stomach** is a thick-walled, J-shaped bag, the widest part of the canal. It receives food from the oesophagus at one end and opens into the small intestine at the other. Its inner lining releases:
- **Mucus** — protects the lining from the acid.
- **Hydrochloric acid** — kills many bacteria that enter with food and makes the medium acidic so the juices can work.
- **Digestive juices** — begin breaking down **proteins** into simpler substances.

The stomach churns food into a semi-liquid paste.

**Did you know?** Much of what we know about the stomach came from an accident. In 1822 a man named Alexis St. Martin was shot in the stomach; the wound healed leaving an opening, through which army doctor William Beaumont observed digestion for years.

check.q: What is the role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
options: Kill bacteria and create an acidic medium for digestion
check.why: Stomach acid kills many bacteria and provides the acidic conditions the digestive juices need.

sections.md:
The **small intestine** is highly coiled and about **7.5 metres** long. It receives juices from three sources:

- **Liver** — the largest gland in the body, reddish-brown, in the upper right of the abdomen. It makes **bile**, stored in a sac called the **gall bladder**. Bile helps digest **fats**.
- **Pancreas** — a large cream-coloured gland just below the stomach. Pancreatic juice acts on carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
- **Intestinal walls** — their own juice completes digestion.

At the end, carbohydrates become simple sugars like **glucose**, fats become **fatty acids and glycerol**, and proteins become **amino acids**.

**Absorption.** The inner wall has thousands of finger-like projections called **villi** (singular: villus). They enormously increase the surface area. Each villus has a network of thin, small blood vessels close to its surface; digested food passes into them and is carried to all parts of the body.

**Assimilation.** In the cells, absorbed substances are used to build complex substances such as proteins. Glucose breaks down with the help of oxygen into carbon dioxide and water, releasing **energy**.

Villi — finger-like projections that absorb food
Assimilation — using absorbed food to build the body

check.q: Villi increase the:
check.why: Villi are finger-like folds that greatly increase the inner surface area so more food is absorbed.

sections.md:
Undigested and unabsorbed food enters the **large intestine**, which is wider but shorter (about 1.5 m). Its main job is to absorb **water and some salts**. The remaining waste is stored in the **rectum** and removed through the **anus** from time to time as faeces. This is **egestion**.

**Diarrhoea.** Sometimes a person has frequent watery stools. Causes include infection, food poisoning and indigestion. It is very common in India, especially among children, and in severe cases can be fatal because the body loses too much water and salt. The first aid is **ORS** — oral rehydration solution: dissolve a pinch of salt and a handful of sugar in a glass of boiled and cooled water (or use an ORS packet as directed). Give it frequently, and see a doctor as soon as possible.

Eating fibre (roughage) — fruits, vegetables, whole grains — keeps the large intestine healthy.

check.q: The main function of the large intestine is to absorb:
check.why: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine; the large intestine mainly recovers water and salts.

sections.md:
Cows, buffaloes and goats seem to chew all day, even while resting. They are **ruminants**. They quickly swallow grass into the first part of their stomach, the **rumen**, where it is partly digested into **cud**. Later the cud returns to the mouth in small lumps and the animal chews it again — **rumination**.

Grass is rich in **cellulose**, a carbohydrate humans cannot digest. Ruminants have bacteria in the rumen that digest cellulose. Many animals including horses and rabbits have a large sac called the **caecum** between the oesophagus... rather, between the small and large intestine, where cellulose-digesting bacteria live. In humans there is no such large caecum and no such bacteria.

This is why a cow can live on grass, but we cannot.

check.q: Why can cattle digest grass but humans cannot?
options: Cattle have bacteria that digest cellulose
check.why: Bacteria in the rumen of cattle break down cellulose, which human digestive juices cannot.

sections.md:
**Amoeba** is a microscopic single-celled organism found in pond water. It has a cell membrane, a rounded dense **nucleus** and many small bubble-like **vacuoles** in its cytoplasm. It keeps changing shape and position by pushing out one or more finger-like projections called **pseudopodia** (false feet), which also help capture food.

Amoeba feeds on microscopic organisms. When it senses food, it pushes out pseudopodia around the food particle and engulfs it, forming a **food vacuole**. Digestive juices are secreted into the vacuole and act on the food, breaking it into simple substances. These are absorbed into the cytoplasm and used for growth, maintenance and multiplication. Undigested residue is expelled outside by the vacuole.

The basic process — ingest, digest, absorb, assimilate, egest — is the same from Amoeba to elephants. Only the equipment differs!

parts.md: Meera won the inter-house quiz and the prize was a samosa from Sharma-ji's canteen. As she bit into it, her science teacher said, "Draw me its journey by Monday." Meera took the challenge seriously. Her incisors cut, her molars ground, and her tongue rolled the crumbs into a soft ball wet with saliva. She noticed the potato beginning to taste faintly sweet — starch turning to sugar.

On her map, the ball slid down the oesophagus in muscular waves into the stomach, where acid and juices worked on the peas' protein for a few hours. Then came the long coiled small intestine, where bile from the liver tackled the oil and pancreatic juice joined in. Villi like a carpet of tiny fingers absorbed glucose and amino acids into her blood. The leftovers — some potato skin fibre — reached the large intestine, which took back water. Her teacher gave the map a star and wrote: "Now draw a cow's version." Meera groaned — and added a rumen.

summary: Animal nutrition: ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, egestion.
Animals feed in many ways — sucking, chewing, swallowing, scraping, capturing; the starfish everts its stomach.
Alimentary canal: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus.
Four kinds of teeth: incisors, canines, premolars, molars; adults have 32; milk teeth fall at 6–8.
Saliva breaks starch into sugar (iodine test shows it).
Tongue mixes food and has taste buds.
Bacterial acids cause tooth decay — brush twice daily.
Stomach makes mucus, HCl and juices that digest proteins.
Liver makes bile (fats), stored in gall bladder; pancreatic juice acts on all food types.
Small intestine (~7.5 m) completes digestion; villi absorb food into blood.
Assimilation builds the body; glucose releases energy.
Large intestine absorbs water and salts; waste leaves via anus.
ORS treats dehydration from diarrhoea.
Ruminants chew cud and digest cellulose with bacteria; caecum in horses/rabbits.

rd-school-c7-science-a.ch03-heat.title: Heat
rd-school-c7-science-a.ch03-heat.subtitle: Why a steel spoon in hot chai burns your fingers but a wooden one doesn't

sections.h: Hot and cold: can we trust our touch?
sections.md:
It is a December morning in Lucknow. You step barefoot on the floor tiles — icy! You step onto the doormat — not so bad. Yet both have been lying in the same room all night. Are they really at different temperatures? This chapter will solve that mystery.

In daily life we meet hot things (tea, a pressure cooker, the noon sun on a road) and cold things (ice, a matka of water, winter air). We decide by touch. But touch is unreliable.

**Activity idea:** Take three mugs: one with tap water, one with warm water (not too hot!), one with ice-cold water. Dip your left hand in the cold mug and your right in the warm mug for two minutes. Now put both hands in the tap-water mug. The left hand says *warm*; the right hand says *cold* — for the same water!

So our sense of touch tells us only whether something is hotter or colder than our skin at that moment. To know *how* hot, we need a reliable measure: **temperature**. Temperature is the degree of hotness of an object, and it is measured with a **thermometer**.

check.q: After keeping one hand in cold and the other in warm water, both put in tap water feel:
check.why: Touch compares an object with your skin's current temperature, so the cooled hand feels the tap water as warm and the warmed hand feels it as cold.

sections.md:
When you have fever, a doctor or parent uses a **clinical thermometer** to read body temperature.

**Its parts:** a long narrow glass tube with a **bulb** at one end. The bulb holds a liquid — traditionally **mercury**, a shiny silvery metal. A **scale** is marked along the tube. A **kink** (small bend) near the bulb stops the mercury from falling back on its own, so you can read the temperature after taking it out of the mouth.

**Range:** a clinical thermometer reads from **35 °C to 42 °C** (some show 94 °F to 108 °F as well). That is because human body temperature normally never goes outside this range.

**Normal body temperature** is about **37 °C** (98.6 °F). It is an average; some healthy people read a little above or below. A temperature of 38 °C or more usually means fever.

**How to read it:**
1. Wash the thermometer, preferably with an antiseptic solution.
2. Hold it firmly and give a few jerks so the mercury falls below 35 °C.
3. Place the bulb under the tongue for about one minute.
4. Take it out and read the level of mercury, keeping it at eye level.

Each large division is usually 1 °C, divided into five small divisions of 0.2 °C each.

**Precautions:** wash before and after use; jerk it down before use; read with the eye in line with the mercury; handle with care — glass breaks; don't hold it by the bulb; never hold it in a flame or hot water.

**Caution box:** Mercury is a toxic substance and very difficult to dispose of if a thermometer breaks. **Digital thermometers**, which use no mercury, are now widely used and are safer.

check.q: Why does a clinical thermometer have a kink?
options: To stop mercury from falling back immediately
check.why: The kink holds the mercury level in place after removal so the reading can be taken.

sections.md:
A clinical thermometer cannot measure the temperature of boiling water or a hot iron — it would break, because its range is only 35–42 °C. For other objects we use a **laboratory thermometer**.

- **Range:** usually **−10 °C to 110 °C**.
- **No kink**, so the mercury falls as soon as it is taken out — the reading must be taken while the bulb is still in the substance.

**How to use it:**
1. Hold it vertically. The bulb must be surrounded by the substance on all sides.
2. The bulb should not touch the bottom or sides of the container.
3. Wait until the mercury thread becomes steady.
4. Read with the eye at the level of the mercury top.

**Did you know?** The highest air temperature in India has been close to 51 °C (Phalodi, Rajasthan, 2016), while Dras in Ladakh can drop below −40 °C in winter. Weather reports also give the **maximum and minimum temperature** of a day, measured with a special maximum–minimum thermometer.

**Celsius and Fahrenheit:** In science we use the Celsius scale (°C). Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at normal pressure. On the Fahrenheit scale, these are 32 °F and 212 °F.

check.q: Why shouldn't you use a clinical thermometer to measure boiling water?
options: Its range is only 35–42 °C and it may break
check.why: Boiling water at 100 °C is far beyond the clinical thermometer's maximum of 42 °C.

sections.md:
Put one end of a steel spoon in a cup of hot chai. Soon the other end feels hot. Heat has travelled. Heat always flows from a **hotter object to a colder one**, and it moves in three ways: **conduction, convection and radiation**.

**Activity idea:** Take an aluminium or iron strip. Fix a few small pieces of wax along it at equal distances. Clamp it on a stand and heat one end with a candle or spirit lamp. The wax pieces melt and fall **one after another**, starting with the one nearest the flame. Heat moved along the strip from the hot end to the cold end.

This transfer of heat through a solid, from its hotter part to its colder part, is **conduction**. In solids, heat is generally transferred by conduction.

**Conductors and insulators.** Materials that let heat pass easily are **conductors**: steel, copper, aluminium, iron. Materials that do not allow heat to pass easily are **poor conductors** or **insulators**: wood, plastic, cloth, cork, air and water. That is why pan handles are made of plastic or wood, and why we use a cloth holder (sansi) to lift hot pots.

Now the mystery of the tiles: the floor tile and the mat are at the same temperature, but tile is a better conductor. It draws heat from your feet quickly, so it *feels* colder.

check.why: Wood does not let heat pass easily, so it is used for handles.

sections.h: Convection: heat that rides on moving liquid and air
sections.md:
How does water in a pan get hot all through, when only the bottom touches the flame? Water is a poor conductor, so it isn't mainly conduction.

**Activity idea:** Put a beaker of water on a burner and drop a crystal of potassium permanganate gently at the bottom. As it heats, a coloured stream **rises** from the crystal, spreads at the top and **sinks** at the sides — a loop.

When water near the flame gets hot, it expands, becomes lighter and **rises**. Cooler water from the sides moves down to take its place, gets heated and rises in turn. This continues until all the water is hot. This mode of heat transfer, by actual movement of the heated material, is **convection**. Liquids and gases are heated mainly by convection.

Air behaves the same way. Hold your hand above a candle flame — it gets hot quickly (hot air rises). Hold it beside the flame — not so hot. Hot air rising is also why smoke goes up a chimney.

**Sea breeze and land breeze.** People in coastal places like Chennai, Mumbai and Puri enjoy a cool breeze. During the **day** the land heats up faster than the water. Air over land becomes hot and rises; cooler air from the sea rushes in to take its place — a **sea breeze**. At **night** the land cools faster than water. Now the air over the sea is warmer and rises; cooler air from the land moves towards the sea — a **land breeze**.

sections.md:
Stand in the winter sun and you feel warm, even though there is no medium touching the sun and you. Heat from the sun crosses about 15 crore kilometres of mostly empty space. It cannot be conduction or convection — both need a material. This third mode, which needs **no medium**, is **radiation**.

All hot bodies radiate heat. You feel warmth when you sit in front of a heater or a bonfire, or put your hand near a hot iron without touching it. A hot cup of tea cools partly by radiating heat to its surroundings. When radiation falls on an object, part is reflected, part absorbed, and part may pass through. The absorbed part warms the object.

**Dark vs light colours.** **Activity idea:** Take two identical tin cans, paint one black and one white (or wrap them in black and white paper). Pour equal amounts of water at the same temperature in both and keep them in the noon sun for an hour. The black can's water is warmer. Now fill both with equal hot water and leave them indoors; the black one also cools faster. Dark surfaces **absorb** more heat — and also radiate it well; light surfaces **reflect** more.

check.q: Heat from the sun reaches the earth by:
check.why: Space between the sun and earth is almost empty, and only radiation needs no medium.

sections.h: Kinds of clothes we wear in summer and winter
sections.md:
Now you can explain your wardrobe with science!

**Summer:** We prefer **light-coloured** clothes, especially white cotton. Light colours reflect most of the sun's heat, so we feel cooler. Cotton also soaks up sweat, which evaporates and cools the body.

**Winter:** We prefer **dark-coloured** clothes because they absorb more heat from the sun. **Woollen** clothes keep us warm. Wool is a poor conductor, and there is **air trapped** between its fibres; air is also a poor conductor. This trapped air stops body heat from flowing out to the cold surroundings.

**Puzzle:** Is it warmer to wear one thick blanket or two thin ones? Two thin blankets are warmer, because a layer of air is trapped between them, adding extra insulation.

**In buildings:** Houses in hot places have thick walls and are often painted white or light colours on the outside. Hollow bricks and terracotta tiles trap air. In cold regions, double walls with air gaps keep houses warm.

**Did you know?** A thermos flask keeps tea hot or juice cold by blocking all three modes: a vacuum stops conduction and convection, and shiny silvered walls reduce radiation.

left.title: Summer clothes
points: Loose and thin for air flow

check.q: Why are woollen clothes warm?
options: Wool fibres trap air, a poor conductor
check.why: Trapped air between wool fibres insulates the body and stops heat escaping.

rd-school-c7-science-a.ch04-acids-bases-.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
rd-school-c7-science-a.ch04-acids-bases-.subtitle: How a turmeric stain on your shirt turned red — and what it was telling you

sections.md:
Paheli spilled dal on her white school shirt. The yellow turmeric stain looked bad, so she scrubbed it with soap. Suddenly the stain turned **reddish-brown**! She panicked. Then, after rinsing with plenty of water, it slowly turned yellow again. What happened? The soap was a **base**, and turmeric is a natural **indicator** that turns red in bases. By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain it — and run your own detective tests in the kitchen.

We use many substances every day: lemon, tamarind (imli), curd, vinegar, baking soda, soap, toothpaste, lime water. Some taste **sour**, some taste **bitter** and feel **soapy** to touch. Taste-testing is not safe in a laboratory, so scientists use other ways to tell them apart.

check.q: Why did the turmeric stain turn red when soap was applied?
options: Soap is a base and turmeric turns red in bases
check.why: Turmeric is a natural indicator that turns red in basic solutions such as soap.

sections.md:
The sour taste of curd, lemon juice, orange juice and vinegar comes from **acids** in them. The word *acid* comes from the Latin *acere*, meaning **sour**. The acids found in these foods are **natural acids**.

Substances like **baking soda** taste bitter and feel soapy when rubbed between fingers. These are **bases**. Their nature is called **basic**.

| Name of acid | Found in |
|---|---|
| Acetic acid | Vinegar |
| Formic acid | Ant's sting |
| Citric acid | Citrus fruits — oranges, lemons |
| Lactic acid | Curd |
| Oxalic acid | Spinach |
| Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) | Amla, citrus fruits |
| Tartaric acid | Tamarind, grapes, unripe mangoes |

| Name of base | Found in |
|---|---|
| Calcium hydroxide | Lime water |
| Ammonium hydroxide | Window cleaner |
| Sodium hydroxide / Potassium hydroxide | Soap |
| Magnesium hydroxide | Milk of magnesia |

**Safety:** Never taste or touch unknown substances in a lab. Some acids and bases, such as hydrochloric acid in a lab or sodium hydroxide, can burn skin.
keyTerms: Acid — sour-tasting substance
Base — bitter, soapy substance
Indicator — substance that changes colour in acid or base

check.q: The acid present in curd is:
check.why: Bacteria turn milk into curd producing lactic acid, which makes curd sour.

sections.md:
So how do we test a substance without tasting it? We use **indicators** — special substances that show a **change in colour** when added to an acidic or basic solution. Turmeric, litmus and China rose petals (gudhal) are **natural indicators**.

**Litmus** is the most common. It is extracted from **lichens**. In distilled water it is mauve (purple). It is available as a solution or as strips of paper, usually red and blue litmus paper.
- **Acid** turns **blue litmus red**.
- **Base** turns **red litmus blue**.
- Solutions that change neither are **neutral** (e.g. distilled water, sugar solution, common salt solution).

**Activity idea:** Make a table of lemon juice, tap water, soap solution, shampoo, salt solution, sugar solution, vinegar, baking soda solution, milk of magnesia, washing soda solution and lime water. Put a drop of each on red and on blue litmus strips with a dropper. Record what changes. Lemon and vinegar redden blue litmus; soap, baking soda and lime water turn red litmus blue; sugar and salt change nothing.

check.why: Only bases change red litmus to blue.

sections.md:
**Turmeric paper:** Take a spoonful of turmeric powder, add a little water to make a paste, and spread it on blotting paper or filter paper. Dry it and cut thin strips. Put a drop of soap solution on a strip — it turns **red**. In acids and neutral solutions, turmeric stays **yellow**. So turmeric tells us only whether something is basic.

This also explains a classic trick: a message written with soap solution on turmeric paper is invisible until... wait, it shows red! Teachers use it as "secret writing".

**China rose (gudhal/hibiscus):** Collect some China rose petals and put them in a beaker of warm water. Leave for some time until the water becomes coloured. Use this coloured water as an indicator. Add five drops to different solutions:
- In **acids**, China rose indicator turns **dark pink (magenta)**.
- In **bases**, it turns **green**.

Other kitchen indicators you can explore: red cabbage juice and beetroot juice also change colour.

**Boojho's question from the chapter:** Is tap water acidic, basic or neutral? Test it with litmus. Usually tap water is close to neutral, but it may be slightly basic or acidic depending on dissolved substances. Distilled water is neutral.

In acid

fig.caption: Natural indicators at a glance.

check.why: China rose turns green in basic solutions, and soap solution is basic.

sections.md:
What happens when an acid meets a base? Let's find out.

**Activity idea:** Fill a quarter of a test tube with dilute hydrochloric acid (done by the teacher). Add 2–3 drops of **phenolphthalein**, a synthetic indicator that stays colourless in acid but turns **pink** in base. Now add dilute sodium hydroxide drop by drop, shaking gently. At one point the solution turns pink. Add one drop of acid — it becomes colourless again. Touch the test tube: it feels **warm**.

The acid and base cancel each other's effect. This reaction is **neutralisation**. It produces **salt and water**, and **heat is released** (the mixture warms up).

> Acid + Base → Salt + Water (+ Heat)

For example:
> Hydrochloric acid + Sodium hydroxide → Sodium chloride (common salt) + Water

The salt formed may be acidic, basic or neutral in nature depending on the acid and base used. **Salts** are a big family; common salt is just one member. Others include washing soda, baking soda, and copper sulphate.

fig.alt: Neutralisation in a test tube

check.q: The products of neutralisation are:
check.why: An acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water, releasing heat.

sections.md:
**Indigestion.** Our stomach contains **hydrochloric acid**, which helps digest food. Too much acid causes indigestion — pain and burning. We take an **antacid** such as **milk of magnesia** (magnesium hydroxide), a base, which neutralises the extra acid. (Take medicines only as advised by a doctor.)

**Ant bite.** An ant's sting injects an acidic liquid, **formic acid**, into the skin. The effect can be neutralised by rubbing moist **baking soda** (sodium hydrogencarbonate) or **calamine** solution, which contains zinc carbonate.

**Soil treatment.** Excessive use of chemical fertilisers makes soil **acidic**. Plants do not grow well in too acidic or too basic soil. If soil is acidic, it is treated with bases like **quick lime** (calcium oxide) or **slaked lime** (calcium hydroxide). If soil is basic, **organic matter (compost)** is added, which releases acids. Farmers test their soil to decide.

**Factory wastes.** Wastes of many factories contain acids. If they flow directly into rivers and lakes, the acids kill fish and other organisms. So factory wastes are **neutralised** by adding basic substances before being discharged.

**Did you know?** Acid rain happens when gases like sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from factories and vehicles dissolve in rain. It damages buildings — the marble of the Taj Mahal is protected partly by controlling pollution in Agra.

check.q: For an ant bite you should apply:
check.why: Baking soda is basic and neutralises the formic acid injected by the ant.

parts.md: On a rainy Sunday, Paheli and Boojho set up a lab on the kitchen table: lemon, vinegar, baking soda, soap, sugar, salt, and a jar of hibiscus water their grandmother had made from garden flowers. "No tasting," said Grandma firmly. They labelled cups and added the hibiscus water drop by drop. Lemon flashed pink; soap turned green; sugar did nothing at all.

Just then an ant bit Boojho's ankle. He yelped. Paheli remembered: ants inject formic acid. She mixed baking soda with a little water and dabbed it on. The sting eased. "That's neutralisation," she said, very pleased. Grandma laughed: "We used to rub it with ash from the chulha — another base!" The two scientists added a new row to their table: Ash — basic.

workedExamples.q: Classify as acidic, basic or neutral: vinegar, lime water, sugar solution.
steps: Vinegar contains acetic acid → reddens blue litmus → acidic.
Lime water is calcium hydroxide → turns red litmus blue → basic.

workedExamples.q: A solution turns turmeric red and China rose green. What will it do to red litmus?
steps: Turmeric red and China rose green both mean base.

workedExamples.q: Three unlabelled bottles hold an acid, a base and distilled water. You have only turmeric. How do you identify them?
steps: Put a drop of each on turmeric paper; the one turning red is the base.
Mix a drop of the base with each of the other two on fresh turmeric: with the acid the red disappears (neutralised); with water the red stays.
So the remaining bottle that removes the red colour is the acid, the last is water.
workedExamples.answer: Use the base found first to tell acid from water

summary: Acids taste sour; bases taste bitter and feel soapy.
Natural acids: acetic (vinegar), citric (lemon), lactic (curd), formic (ant sting), tartaric (tamarind), oxalic (spinach), ascorbic (amla).
Bases: lime water, soap, milk of magnesia, window cleaner (ammonium hydroxide).
Never taste unknown substances.

Litmus comes from lichens: acid turns blue litmus red; base turns red litmus blue.
Turmeric turns red in base; yellow otherwise.

Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid, pink in base.
Uses: antacids for indigestion, baking soda for ant bites, lime for acidic soil, compost for basic soil, treating factory waste.

Neither acidic nor basic.

rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch01-environme.title: Environment
rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch01-environme.subtitle: Everything around you — and how it is all connected

sections.md:
Imagine a boy named Ravi on a summer holiday in a village near Nashik. He walks out of his house and makes a list: the mango tree, a cow, his neighbour's grandmother, the well, the river beyond the fields, the road, the bus, the school, the temple, the sun overhead and the air he breathes. Some of these were made by nature; some by people; and he and his neighbours are part of the list too.

The word **environment** comes from the French word *environner*, meaning **neighbourhood** or surroundings. Our surroundings — the places, things and nature — are our environment. It is a combination of **natural** and **human-made** phenomena.

- The **natural environment** consists of land, water, air, plants and animals.
- The **human-made environment** consists of the things humans create: buildings, parks, bridges, roads, industries, monuments.
- The **human environment** is the interaction of people with each other and with their surroundings — family, community, religion, economic activity, education.

The environment is our **basic life support system**. It provides the air we breathe, the water we drink, the food we eat and the land where we live.

sections.md:
Geographers divide the natural environment into four interconnected domains:

**1. Lithosphere** — the solid crust or hard top layer of the earth. It is made of rocks and minerals and covered by a thin layer of soil. It has landforms such as mountains, plateaus, plains and valleys. Landforms are found on continents and on the ocean floor too. The lithosphere gives us forests, grasslands for grazing, land for agriculture and settlements, and is a rich source of minerals.

**2. Hydrosphere** — the domain of water. It includes oceans, rivers, lakes, ice in glaciers, underground water and water vapour in the air. All living things need water. About three-fourths of the earth's surface is covered by water.

**3. Atmosphere** — the thin layer of air surrounding the earth. The gravitational force of the earth holds it. It protects us from harmful rays and scorching heat of the sun. It contains gases like nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide, plus dust and water vapour. Changes in the atmosphere produce changes in weather and climate.

**4. Biosphere** — the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and interact to support life. It includes the **plant kingdom** and the **animal kingdom**, including humans.

head: Domain
Meaning
Examples
fig.caption: Four domains of the natural environment.

keyTerms: Lithosphere — solid outer layer of the earth
Hydrosphere — water on and around the earth
Atmosphere — blanket of air
Biosphere — the zone of life

check.why: The biosphere is the life-supporting zone where the other three domains meet.

sections.h: Ecosystem: a web of give and take
sections.md:
All plants, animals and humans depend on their immediate surroundings, and often on each other. A system formed by the interaction of all living organisms with each other and with the physical environment is called an **ecosystem**.

An ecosystem can be **large** — a rainforest, a grassland, a desert, an ocean — or **small** — a pond, a tree, a garden, even a puddle.

Think of a pond in a village. Sunlight helps algae and water plants grow. Small insects and fish eat the plants. Frogs eat insects; kingfishers and snakes eat frogs and fish. When plants and animals die, tiny decomposers break them down and return nutrients to the water and mud. The water, mud, air and sunlight are the **non-living** part; the plants and animals are the **living** part. Remove one link — say, the pond is polluted and fish die — and the kingfishers leave too.

**Activity idea from the chapter:** Draw a food chain you see near your school, such as grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle. Each animal depends on the one before it.

sections.md:
Human beings interact with the environment and modify it according to their needs.

**Early humans** adapted themselves to their natural surroundings. They led a simple life and fulfilled their needs from nature: food from hunting and gathering, shelter in caves, clothing from leaves and animal skins. Their needs were very few.

With time, needs grew. Humans learnt new ways to use and change the environment:
- They learnt to grow crops, domesticate animals and lead a settled life.
- The **wheel** was invented, surplus food was produced, and **barter** (exchange of goods) began; trade started.
- **Commerce** developed. The **Industrial Revolution** enabled large-scale production.
- **Transportation** became faster. The **information revolution** made communication easier and quicker across the world.

The human environment includes religion, education, economic activities, community, and the way we live together.

**Did you know?** The **Industrial Revolution** began in Britain in the 18th century, with machines like the steam engine. It changed how goods were made, but also increased the use of coal and pollution.

check.q: Barter means:
check.why: Barter is the direct exchange of goods for goods, used before money became common.

sections.h: A perfect balance — and how we disturb it
sections.md:
There is a perfect balance between the natural and human environments. But as humans build cities, factories, dams and roads, the natural environment gets modified. Sometimes this improves life; often it causes problems:

- **Air pollution** from vehicles and factories — look at Delhi's winter smog.
- **Water pollution** when sewage and industrial waste enter rivers.
- **Land degradation** from deforestation, mining and overuse of chemicals.
- **Loss of habitat** for animals, pushing species towards extinction.
- **Climate change** from burning coal, oil and gas.

A small change in one domain disturbs others: cutting forests on hills increases soil erosion (lithosphere), floods and silted rivers (hydrosphere), local temperature and rainfall changes (atmosphere) and loss of birds and animals (biosphere).

People have increasingly understood this and are acting to protect the environment: planting trees, saving water, using public transport, recycling, reducing plastic, using solar energy.

**World Environment Day** is celebrated on **5 June** every year to spread awareness about protecting the environment.

check.q: World Environment Day is observed on:
check.why: 5 June is World Environment Day, observed worldwide to promote care for the environment.

sections.md:
**The village that saved its trees.** In the 1970s, in the hills of present-day Uttarakhand, villagers — many of them women — hugged trees to stop them from being cut. This became famous as the **Chipko movement**. Long before that, in 1730, the **Bishnoi** community of Khejarli in Rajasthan, led by Amrita Devi, gave their lives to protect khejri trees. These stories show communities caring for their environment.

**A river story.** A river flowing past a town provides drinking water, fish and irrigation. If the town dumps garbage and sewage into it, fish die, people downstream fall ill and the river smells. Cleaning drives, sewage treatment plants and public awareness can restore it.

**Activity idea:** Survey your locality. List the natural, human-made and human elements. Note one environmental problem and suggest two ways to solve it. Discuss in class.

**What can you do?** Switch off lights and fans when not needed, close taps, carry a cloth bag, segregate wet and dry waste, plant a sapling and look after it, and cycle or walk for short distances.

check.q: The Chipko movement was about:
check.why: Villagers hugged trees to stop them from being felled, protecting their forest environment.

summary: Environment means our surroundings; from French 'environner' (neighbourhood).
It includes natural, human-made and human components.
Natural environment: land, water, air, plants, animals.
Human-made: buildings, roads, bridges, parks, industries.
Lithosphere is the solid crust with rocks, minerals, soil and landforms.
Hydrosphere is the domain of water; ~three-fourths of surface.
Atmosphere is the air blanket held by gravity; it protects us and gives weather.
Biosphere is the zone where land, water and air support life.
An ecosystem is the interaction of living things with each other and their surroundings.
Early humans adapted to nature; later humans modified it through farming, trade, industry and technology.
Human activities can disturb the balance: pollution, deforestation, climate change.
World Environment Day: 5 June.
Communities like the Bishnois and Chipko activists protected trees.

glossary.d: All our surroundings, natural and human-made.
Living things interacting with each other and their physical surroundings.
Exchange of goods without money.
Shift to machine-based mass production from the 18th century.

rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch02-inside-ou.title: Inside Our Earth
rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch02-inside-ou.subtitle: A journey 6,000 km down — and the rocks that tell the earth's story

sections.h: Can we dig to the other side?
sections.md:
Every child has wondered: if I dig a hole in my garden in Bengaluru and keep going, where will I come out? The earth is about **6,371 km** to its centre. The deepest mine in the world, in South Africa, goes only about **4 km** down. The deepest hole ever drilled (in Russia) reached about **12 km**. To reach the centre we would need to dig more than 6,000 km through rock hotter than a furnace. So how do we know what lies inside?

Scientists study the way **earthquake waves** travel through the earth, the lava thrown up by **volcanoes**, the density of the earth and **meteorites** that reach us from space. Just as a doctor uses X-rays to see inside a body, these clues let us "see" inside our planet.

Like an onion, the earth is made of several concentric layers, one inside another.

check.q: About how far is it to the centre of the earth?
check.why: The earth's radius is about 6,371 km, so the centre lies more than 6,000 km below us.

sections.h: Interior of the earth: crust, mantle, core
sections.md:
**1. The crust** — the uppermost layer, on which we live. It is the **thinnest** of all layers. It is about **35 km** thick on the continental masses but only about **5 km** on the ocean floors.

- The main mineral constituents of the **continental mass** are **silica and alumina** — so it is called **sial** (si = silica, al = alumina).
- The **oceanic crust** mainly consists of **silica and magnesium** — called **sima** (si = silica, ma = magnesium).

**2. The mantle** — just beneath the crust, extending up to a depth of about **2,900 km** below the crust.

**3. The core** — the innermost layer, with a radius of about **3,500 km**. It is mainly made of **nickel and iron** — called **nife** (ni = nickel, fe = ferrous, i.e. iron). The central core has very high temperature and pressure. The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid.

Here's a striking fact: the crust forms only **1 per cent** of the volume of the earth, **84 per cent** consists of the mantle and **15 per cent** makes the core.

**Did you know?** If the earth were an apple, the crust would be thinner than the apple's skin.

keyTerms: Sial — silica + alumina: continental crust
Sima — silica + magnesium: oceanic crust
Nife — nickel + iron: core

check.q: The core of the earth is mainly made of:
check.why: The core is called nife because it is mostly nickel (ni) and iron (fe).

sections.md:
The earth's crust is made of various types of rocks. Any natural mass of mineral matter that makes up the earth's crust is called a **rock**. Rocks can be of different colour, size and texture. Some are hard like granite; some are soft like soapstone; some are made of tiny grains of sand.

There are three major types of rocks: **igneous**, **sedimentary** and **metamorphic**.

**Igneous rocks.** When molten magma cools, it becomes solid. Rocks thus formed are called **igneous** (from the Latin *ignis*, fire) or **primary rocks**. There are two types:
- **Extrusive igneous rocks:** When molten lava comes out onto the earth's surface, it cools rapidly and becomes solid. These rocks have a very **fine-grained** structure. Example: **basalt**. The **Deccan plateau** is made of basalt rocks.
- **Intrusive igneous rocks:** Sometimes the molten magma cools down **deep inside** the earth's crust. Solid rocks so formed are called intrusive. Since they cool slowly they form **large grains**. Example: **granite**. Grinding stones used to prepare paste and powder of spices and grains are often made of granite.

check.q: Basalt is an example of:
check.why: Basalt forms when lava cools quickly on the surface, making it extrusive igneous rock.

sections.md:
Rocks roll down, crack, and hit each other, breaking down into small fragments. These smaller particles are called **sediments**. Wind, water and ice carry them and deposit them in layers. These loose sediments get compressed and hardened over long periods to form layers of rocks. These are called **sedimentary rocks** (from the Latin *sedimentum*, settle down).

Example: **sandstone** is made from grains of sand. Shale, limestone and conglomerate are other sedimentary rocks.

Sedimentary rocks may also contain **fossils** — the remains of dead plants and animals trapped in the layers of rocks. Fossils tell us about life millions of years ago. Fossils of dinosaurs and their eggs have been found in places like Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.

**Did you know?** The famous Red Fort in Delhi and many Mughal buildings were built with red sandstone from places like Fatehpur Sikri.

check.q: Fossils are most likely to be found in:
check.why: Fossils are preserved as remains get buried in layers of sediment that harden into sedimentary rock.

sections.md:
Igneous and sedimentary rocks can change into **metamorphic rocks** under great **heat and pressure** (from the Greek *metamorphose*, change of form).

- **Clay** changes into **slate**.
- **Limestone** changes into **marble**.

Marble is white and beautiful; the **Taj Mahal** in Agra is built of white marble brought from Makrana in Rajasthan. Slate is used for roofing and, in older days, for children's writing slates.

The three rock types are connected. Think of a family where members keep changing form over millions of years.

check.q: Limestone changes into marble due to:
check.why: Great heat and pressure transform limestone into the metamorphic rock marble.

sections.md:
One type of rock changes to another type under certain conditions in a cyclic manner. This process of transformation of rock from one to another is called the **rock cycle**.

1. Molten **magma** cools and solidifies to become **igneous** rock.
2. Igneous rocks break down into small particles, which are transported and deposited to form **sedimentary** rocks.
3. When igneous and sedimentary rocks are subjected to heat and pressure, they change into **metamorphic** rocks.
4. Metamorphic rocks, under great heat and pressure, can **melt** down to form molten magma again — and the cycle restarts.

Sedimentary and metamorphic rocks can also be broken into sediments, forming new sedimentary rocks.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#fbf5ec'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle'><circle cx='300' cy='50' r='40' fill='#f08a24'/><text x='300' y='55' fill='#fff'>Magma</text><circle cx='490' cy='170' r='46' fill='#7a7a7a'/><text x='490' y='175' fill='#fff'>Igneous</text><circle cx='300' cy='275' r='42' fill='#d7b46a'/><text x='300' y='280'>Sedimentary</text><circle cx='110' cy='170' r='46' fill='#8b6db3'/><text x='110' y='175' fill='#fff'>Metamorphic</text></g><path id='cyc' d='M340 60 Q470 80 480 125 M470 210 Q420 270 345 275 M255 275 Q160 260 125 215 M120 125 Q170 60 260 55' fill='none' stroke='#444' stroke-width='2'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='11' fill='#333'><text x='420' y='80'>cooling</text><text x='410' y='265'>weathering, deposition</text><text x='110' y='265'>heat, pressure</text><text x='130' y='80'>melting</text></g><circle r='7' fill='#e33'><animateMotion dur='8s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M300 90 Q450 100 470 150 Q440 260 300 233 Q160 250 140 170 Q160 90 300 90'/></circle></svg>

fig.alt: Animated rock cycle

check.q: In the rock cycle, metamorphic rocks can melt to form:
check.why: Under great heat and pressure metamorphic rocks melt into magma, restarting the cycle.

sections.h: Minerals and the uses of rocks
sections.md:
Rocks are made of different **minerals**. Minerals are naturally occurring substances which have certain physical properties and a definite chemical composition. Minerals are very important to humankind:
- Some are used as **fuels**: coal, natural gas and petroleum.
- They are used in **industries**: iron, aluminium, gold, uranium.
- They are used in **medicine** and in **fertilisers**.

Rocks are useful too. Hard rocks are used for making **roads, houses and buildings**. We use stones in many games: hopscotch (stapu/kit-kit), seven stones (pitthoo) and five stones (gitti). In earlier times stones were used to make tools.

**Did you know?** In India, the Chota Nagpur plateau is rich in coal, iron and other minerals; Rajasthan is known for marble and sandstone; Kolar in Karnataka was famous for gold.

**Activity idea:** Collect pebbles and stones from your surroundings. Sort them by colour, weight and texture and try to guess their type. Visit a museum's geology gallery if you can.

check.q: Which of these minerals is used as a fuel?
check.why: Coal is a mineral fuel burnt to release energy.

parts.md: I was born in fire, 6.5 crore years ago, when lava poured out over the Deccan and cooled quickly into black basalt — that's me. For ages I lay in the sun and monsoon, cracking a little each year. Rain carried my crumbs into a river, and the river dropped them in quiet layers at the bottom of a lake. Squeezed under more layers, my crumbs hardened into rock again — sedimentary now, with a tiny snail shell pressed inside me as a fossil.

Then the earth's plates pushed and heated me deep underground; I changed form once more and became metamorphic. One day, perhaps, I will melt into magma and begin again. For now a girl named Asha has picked me up from a stream near Pune and put me on her desk. She wrote a label: 'Igneous? Sedimentary? Metamorphic? All three!' She's right — I am the rock cycle in one pebble.

summary: Earth's radius is about 6,371 km; we know its interior from earthquake waves, volcanoes and meteorites.
Three layers: crust, mantle, core.
Crust: thinnest; ~35 km under continents, ~5 km under oceans.
Continental crust = sial; oceanic crust = sima.
Mantle extends to ~2,900 km below the crust.
Core: radius ~3,500 km; nife (nickel + iron).
Volume: crust 1%, mantle 84%, core 15%.
Rocks: natural masses of mineral matter; three types.
Igneous: extrusive (basalt, fine grains) and intrusive (granite, large grains).
Sedimentary: from deposited sediments; e.g. sandstone; may hold fossils.
Metamorphic: from heat and pressure; clay → slate, limestone → marble.
Rock cycle: continuous change from one rock type to another.
Minerals have definite composition; used as fuels, in industry, medicine and fertilisers.

glossary.d: Molten rock inside the earth.
Magma that comes out on the surface.
Small rock particles carried and deposited.
Remains of ancient plants or animals in rock.
Natural substance with definite composition.
Transformation of rocks from one type to another.

rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch03-our-chang.title: Our Changing Earth
rd-school-c7-social-a.geo-ch03-our-chang.subtitle: Earthquakes, volcanoes, rivers, waves, glaciers and wind — the sculptors of our planet

sections.md:
On the morning of 26 January 2001, while Gujarat was celebrating Republic Day, the ground at Bhuj shook violently. Buildings collapsed in seconds and thousands of lives were lost. How can solid ground move?

The earth's crust is not one single unbroken shell. The **lithosphere** is broken into a number of large and small pieces called **lithospheric plates**. These plates move around very slowly — just a few millimetres each year — because of the movement of the molten **magma** inside the earth. The molten magma moves in a circular manner (like boiling dal in a pot).

The movement of these plates causes changes on the surface. Earth movements are divided on the basis of the forces that cause them:
- **Endogenic forces** act in the interior of the earth.
- **Exogenic forces** work on the surface of the earth.

Endogenic forces sometimes produce **sudden movements** (earthquakes, volcanoes) and at other times **slow movements** (building mountains over millions of years). Exogenic forces wear down and build up the surface.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='240' fill='#fdf2e5'/><rect x='0' y='150' width='600' height='90' fill='#e5793b'/><g fill='none' stroke='#fff3' stroke-width='3'><ellipse cx='150' cy='195' rx='90' ry='25'/><ellipse cx='450' cy='195' rx='90' ry='25'/></g><g><rect x='30' y='110' width='260' height='40' fill='#8c6a46'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;12 0;0 0' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect><rect x='310' y='110' width='260' height='40' fill='#6f8c46'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-12 0;0 0' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='#222'><text x='90' y='100'>plate A →</text><text x='410' y='100'>← plate B</text><text x='230' y='225' fill='#fff'>magma moves in circles</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Lithospheric plates ride slowly on circulating magma.
fig.alt: Moving plates on magma

check.q: Forces that act in the interior of the earth are called:
check.why: Endogenic means originating inside, so these forces act in the earth's interior.

sections.md:
A **volcano** is a vent (opening) in the earth's crust through which molten material erupts suddenly. Magma, gases, ash and rock fragments are thrown out; magma that reaches the surface is called **lava**. Over time, layers of lava and ash may build a cone-shaped mountain around the vent.

India's only active volcano is on **Barren Island** in the Andaman Sea. Famous volcanoes elsewhere include Mount Vesuvius (Italy), whose eruption in 79 CE buried the town of Pompeii, and Mount Fuji (Japan).

The Deccan plateau itself was formed from huge lava flows millions of years ago.

check.q: India's only active volcano is on:
check.why: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has India's only active volcano.

sections.md:
When the lithospheric plates move, the surface of the earth **vibrates**. The vibrations can travel all around the earth. These vibrations are called **earthquakes**.

- The place in the crust **where the movement starts** is called the **focus**.
- The place on the surface **directly above the focus** is called the **epicentre**.
- Vibrations travel outwards from the epicentre as waves. Greatest damage is usually closest to the epicentre, and the strength decreases away from it.

Earthquakes cannot be predicted exactly, but their impact can be reduced by being prepared. They are measured with a machine called a **seismograph**. The magnitude is measured on the **Richter scale**. An earthquake of 2.0 or less can hardly be felt; above 5.0 causes damage from falling objects; 6.0 or more is very strong and 7.0 or above is a major earthquake. The 2001 Bhuj earthquake measured about 7.7.

**Did you know? Traditional warning signs.** People in some communities watched animal behaviour — rats come out of burrows, fish in ponds agitated, snakes come to the surface, birds restless — as possible signs. These are not reliable scientific predictions, but they are part of local knowledge.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 280' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='280' fill='#eef3fa'/><rect x='0' y='90' width='600' height='190' fill='#b98a5e'/><circle cx='300' cy='210' r='7' fill='#d22'/><text x='312' y='215' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>focus</text><line x1='300' y1='210' x2='300' y2='90' stroke='#333' stroke-dasharray='4 4'/><text x='265' y='80' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'>epicentre</text><g fill='none' stroke='#fff' stroke-width='2'><circle cx='300' cy='210' r='10'><animate attributeName='r' values='10;200' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><circle cx='300' cy='210' r='10'><animate attributeName='r' values='10;200' dur='3s' begin='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='opacity' values='1;0' dur='3s' begin='1.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle></g><g><rect x='130' y='50' width='30' height='40' fill='#666'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' values='-3 145 90;3 145 90;-3 145 90' dur='0.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></rect></g></svg>
fig.caption: Waves spread from the focus; the epicentre is the surface point just above it.
fig.alt: Focus and epicentre of an earthquake

check.q: The point on the surface directly above the focus is the:
check.why: The epicentre lies on the surface right above the focus where the movement began.

sections.md:
**Safe places:** under a strong table or kitchen counter, against an inside wall. Stay away from fireplaces, windows, mirrors and picture frames, and heavy objects that can fall.

**Drop, cover and hold on:** drop to the floor, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Protect your head and neck.

**If outdoors:** move to an open area, away from buildings, trees, electric poles and overhead wires.

**Be prepared:** spread awareness among friends and family. Keep an emergency kit with water, a torch, a first-aid box and important papers. Schools should hold earthquake drills.

In earthquake-prone areas, buildings should follow earthquake-resistant designs. Japan, which has many earthquakes, builds houses that sway but do not collapse.

check.q: During an earthquake indoors, the safest action is:
options: Drop, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on
check.why: Covering under a sturdy table protects you from falling objects until the shaking stops.

sections.md:
The landscape is being continuously worn by two processes — **weathering** and **erosion**.

- **Weathering** is the breaking up of rocks on the earth's surface (by heat, cold, rain, plant roots).
- **Erosion** is the wearing away of the landscape by different agents like **water, wind and ice**. The eroded material is carried away and finally **deposited**.

This process of erosion and deposition creates different landforms on the earth's surface. Let us follow each agent in turn: **rivers, sea waves, glaciers and wind**.

check.q: Breaking up of rocks on the surface is called:
check.why: Weathering is the in-place breaking of rocks, while erosion carries the material away.

sections.md:
The running water in a river erodes the landscape.

- **Waterfall:** When a river tumbles at a steep angle over very hard rocks or down a steep valley side, it forms a waterfall. The **Angel Falls** of Venezuela is the highest waterfall in the world. Others are Niagara Falls (USA–Canada border) and Victoria Falls (Africa). In India, Jog Falls in Karnataka is famous.
- **Meanders:** As the river enters the plain, it twists and turns, forming large bends called meanders.
- **Ox-bow lake:** Due to continuous erosion and deposition along the sides of a meander, the ends of the loop come closer. In time the loop cuts off from the river and forms a cut-off lake, also called an ox-bow lake.
- **Floodplain:** At times the river overflows its banks. This leads to flooding, and layers of fine soil and other material called **sediments** are deposited along its banks, making a flat, fertile **floodplain**.
- **Levees:** The raised banks formed along the river by deposition.
- **Distributaries and delta:** As the river approaches the sea, its speed falls and it breaks into a number of streams called distributaries. The river becomes so slow that it deposits its load. Each distributary forms its own mouth. The collection of sediments from all the mouths forms a **delta** — like the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta (Sundarbans), the world's largest.

fig.alt: River landforms

check.q: A cut-off meander loop forms a/an:
check.why: When a meander loop is cut off from the main channel it becomes an ox-bow lake.

sections.md:
The erosion and deposition of sea waves give rise to coastal landforms.

- **Sea caves:** Sea waves continuously strike the rocks. Cracks develop and become larger over time, forming hollow-like caves.
- **Sea arches:** As cavities become bigger and bigger, only the roof of the caves remains, forming an arch.
- **Stacks:** Erosion breaks the roof and only walls are left. These wall-like features are called stacks.
- **Sea cliff:** The steep rocky coast rising almost vertically above sea water.
- **Beaches:** Sea waves deposit sediments along the shores, forming beaches — like Marina Beach, Chennai, or the beaches of Goa.

fig.caption: How waves carve coasts over time.

check.q: When the roof of a sea arch collapses, what remains is a:
check.why: The standing wall-like pillar left after the arch's roof falls is a stack.

sections.md:
**Glaciers** are "rivers" of ice. They erode the landscape by bulldozing soil and stones to expose the solid rock below. Glaciers carve out deep hollows; as the ice melts they get filled with water and become beautiful lakes in the mountains. The material carried by the glacier — rocks big and small, sand and silt — gets deposited. These deposits form **glacial moraines**. The Gangotri glacier is the source of the Ganga.

**Wind** is an active agent of erosion and deposition in **deserts**.
- **Mushroom rocks:** Winds erode the lower section of a rock more than the upper part. The rock gets a narrower base and wider top — like a mushroom.
- **Sand dunes:** When wind blows, it lifts and transports sand. When it stops blowing, the sand falls and is deposited in low hill-like structures called sand dunes (seen in the Thar desert).
- **Loess:** When the grains of sand are very fine and light, wind can carry them over very long distances. When such sand is deposited in large areas, it is called loess. Large deposits of loess are found in **China**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 220' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='220' fill='#fff3d6'/><path d='M0 180 Q80 130 160 180 Q240 120 330 180 L330 220 L0 220Z' fill='#e7c07a'/><path d='M420 180 L440 120 Q400 110 410 90 Q470 60 530 90 Q540 112 500 120 L520 180Z' fill='#b97a4b'/><g stroke='#c9a35f' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'><line x1='0' y1='150' x2='40' y2='150'><animate attributeName='x1' values='-40;600' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='x2' values='0;640' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line><line x1='0' y1='165' x2='30' y2='165'><animate attributeName='x1' values='-60;600' dur='2.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><animate attributeName='x2' values='-30;630' dur='2.4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='110' y='210'>sand dunes</text><text x='430' y='205'>mushroom rock</text></g></svg>

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch01-tracing-.title: Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch01-tracing-.subtitle: How two old maps, a scribe's mistakes and a word like 'Hindustan' help us read 700–1750 CE

sections.md:
Picture two maps of the subcontinent side by side.

**Map 1** was made in **1154 CE** by the Arab geographer **al-Idrisi** for a king in Sicily. It looks strange to us: south India is at the place where we would expect north India, and Sri Lanka is the island at the top. Place-names are in **Arabic**, and some familiar names like Kanauj in Uttar Pradesh are spelt *Qanauj*. This is because mapmakers in that tradition put the **south at the top** — not wrong, just a different convention.

**Map 2** was made in the **1720s** by a **French** cartographer. It looks much more familiar: the coastal areas especially are surprisingly detailed. By this time European sailors and merchants used such maps for their voyages.

Why do the two maps differ so much? Over about 600 years **the science of cartography** changed, and the **information available** to the mapmakers was different. So when historians read documents, maps and texts from the past, they must be sensitive to the **contexts** in which the information was produced.

left.title: al-Idrisi, 1154
points: Made for a king of Sicily

check.q: Why does al-Idrisi's map look 'upside down' to us?
options: He followed a tradition of putting south at the top
Sri Lanka was in the north
check.why: Mapmaking conventions differed, and al-Idrisi's tradition placed the south at the top.

sections.h: New and old terminology: what did 'Hindustan' mean?
sections.md:
Words and their meanings change over time.

Today we understand **Hindustan** as India, the modern nation-state. But when the term was used in the 13th century by **Minhaj-i Siraj**, a chronicler who wrote in Persian, he meant the areas of **Punjab, Haryana and the lands between the Ganga and Yamuna**. He used the term in a **political** sense for lands that were part of the dominions of the **Delhi Sultan**. The areas included changed with the extent of the Sultanate, but the term never included **south India**.

By contrast, in the early 16th century **Babur** used Hindustan to describe the **geography, fauna and culture** of the inhabitants of the subcontinent. This was somewhat like the way the 14th-century poet **Amir Khusrau** used the word **Hind**. So while the idea of a geographical and cultural entity like "India" did exist, the term Hindustan did not carry the political and national meanings it has today.

**The word 'foreigner'.** Today it means someone not Indian. In the medieval period, a "foreigner" was **any stranger** who appeared, for example, in a village — someone not part of that society or culture. A city-dweller might regard a forest-dweller as a foreigner, but two peasants of the same village were not foreigners to each other even if they had different religious or caste backgrounds. In Hindi the term *pardesi* and in Persian *ajnabi* expressed this idea.

check.q: For Minhaj-i Siraj, 'Hindustan' meant:
options: Punjab, Haryana and the Ganga–Yamuna lands under the Delhi Sultan
check.why: He used it politically for the Delhi Sultan's lands in the north, never including south India.

sections.md:
Historians use different types of sources depending on the period they study and the nature of their investigation. For the period 700–1750 they still rely on **coins, inscriptions, architecture and textual records**, but there is also considerable continuity — and some important new things.

The number and variety of **textual records increased dramatically** during this period. They slowly displaced other types of available information. Why? **Paper** gradually became cheaper and more widely available. People used it to write holy texts, chronicles of rulers, letters and teachings of saints, petitions and judicial records, and for registers of accounts and taxes.

Manuscripts were collected by wealthy people, rulers, monasteries and temples. They were placed in libraries and archives. These manuscripts and documents give historians a lot of detailed information, but they are also **difficult to use**.

**Did you know?** In the 13th century, paper was so precious that a scholar might write a manuscript, wash off the ink and reuse the paper. By the 16th century it was much cheaper — a person could buy a large ream of paper with very little money.

check.q: Why did the number of written records increase in this period?
options: Paper became cheaper and more widely available
check.why: Cheaper paper allowed more chronicles, letters, petitions and accounts to be written.

sections.h: The problem of manuscripts: copying by hand
sections.md:
There was **no printing press** in those days, so **scribes copied manuscripts by hand**. Copying was not an easy task. As scribes copied, they also introduced **small changes** — a word here, a sentence there. These small differences grew over centuries of copying until manuscripts of the same text became substantially different from one another.

This is a serious problem because we rarely find the original manuscript of the author today. We are totally dependent upon the copies made by later scribes. As a result, historians have to read **different manuscript versions** of the same text to guess what the author had originally written.

On occasion, authors themselves revised their chronicles at different times. The 14th-century chronicler **Ziyauddin Barani** wrote his chronicle first in **1356** and another version **two years later**. The two differ from each other, but historians did not know about the existence of the first version until the 1960s. It remained lost in large library collections.
