sections.md:
The thousand years between 700 and 1750 were a time of great change. Several **technological changes** made their appearance: the **Persian wheel** in irrigation, the **spinning wheel** in weaving, and **firearms** in combat. **New foods and beverages** arrived in the subcontinent: **potatoes, corn (maize), chillies, tea and coffee**. Many of these came from the Americas, which Europeans reached around 1500.

These changes came along with new people who brought in new ideas too. As a result, this was a period of **economic, political, social and cultural changes**.

One of the most important groups was the **Rajputs**, a name derived from *rajaputra*, the son of a ruler. Between the 8th and 14th centuries the term applied more generally to a group of warriors who claimed Kshatriya caste status. It included not just rulers and chieftains but also soldiers and commanders who served in the armies of different monarchs. A chivalric code — extreme valour and a great sense of loyalty — was attributed to Rajputs by their poets and bards.

Other groups such as the **Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Ahoms and Kayasthas** (a caste of scribes and secretaries) also used the opportunities of the age to become politically important.

check.q: Which of these came to the subcontinent in this period?
options: Potatoes, maize, chillies, tea and coffee
check.why: These crops and beverages were new arrivals, many from the Americas.

sections.md:
Throughout this period there was a gradual **clearing of forests** and the **extension of agriculture** — a change faster in some areas than others. Changes in their habitat forced many **forest-dwellers to migrate**. Others started tilling the land and became **peasants**. These new peasant groups gradually began to be influenced by **regional markets, chieftains, priests, monasteries and temples**. They became part of large, complex societies and were required to pay taxes and offer goods and services to local lords.

As a result, significant economic and social differences emerged amongst peasants. Some possessed more productive land, others also kept cattle, and some combined artisanal work with agricultural activity during the lean season.

As society became more differentiated, people were grouped into **jatis** or sub-castes and ranked on the basis of their backgrounds and their occupations. Ranks were not fixed permanently; they varied according to the power, influence and resources controlled by members of the jati. The status of the same jati could vary from area to area.

Jatis framed their **own rules and regulations** to manage the conduct of their members. These regulations were enforced by an **assembly of elders**, described in some areas as the **jati panchayat**. But jatis were also required to follow the rules of their villages. Several villages were governed by a chieftain. Together they were only one small unit of a state.

check.q: Jati rules were enforced by:
options: An assembly of elders called the jati panchayat
check.why: Each jati had an assembly of elders, often called the jati panchayat, to enforce its rules.

sections.md:
Large states like those of the **Cholas, Tughluqs or Mughals** encompassed many regions.

A Sanskrit **prashasti** (praise poem) praising the Delhi Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Balban** (1266–1287) explained that he was the ruler of a vast empire that stretched from **Bengal (Gauda)** in the east to **Ghazni (Gajjana)** in Afghanistan in the west and included all of south India (Dravida). People of different regions — Gauda, Andhra, Kerala, Karnata, Maharashtra and Gujarat — apparently fled before his armies. Historians regard these as **exaggerated claims** of conquest. At the same time, they try to understand why rulers kept claiming to have control over different parts of the subcontinent.

By 700, many regions already possessed distinct **geographical dimensions** and their own **language and cultural characteristics**. They were also associated with specific **ruling dynasties**. There was considerable conflict between these states. Occasionally dynasties like the Cholas, Khaljis, Tughluqs and Mughals built empires that were **pan-regional** — spanning diverse regions. Not all these empires were equally stable or successful.

When the Mughal Empire declined in the 18th century, it led to the re-emergence of **regional states**. But years of imperial, pan-regional rule had altered the character of the regions. Across most of the subcontinent, regions were left with the legacies of the big and small states that had ruled over them — apparent in distinct and shared traditions in governance, management of the economy, elite cultures and language. Through the thousand years, regions did not grow in isolation; while retaining their distinctiveness, they felt the impact of larger pan-regional forces of integration.

check.q: Historians treat the prashasti's claims about Balban's empire as:
check.why: Praise poems inflated conquests, so historians read them as exaggerations while asking why rulers made such claims.

sections.md:
During this thousand years, important developments took place in religious traditions. People's belief in the divine was sometimes deeply personal, but more usually it was **collective**. Collective belief was often influenced by the social, economic and political organisation of local communities.

**Changes in Hinduism** included the worship of **new deities**, the construction of **temples** by royalty and the growing importance of **Brahmanas** (priests) as dominant groups in society. Their knowledge of Sanskrit texts earned them respect, and their dominant position was consolidated by the support of their patrons — new rulers searching for prestige.

One of the major developments was the emergence of the idea of **bhakti** — of a loving, personal deity that devotees could reach without the aid of priests or elaborate rituals.

This was also the period when **new religions** appeared. **Merchants and migrants** first brought the teachings of the holy **Quran** to India in the 7th century. Muslims regard the Quran as their holy book and accept the sovereignty of one God, **Allah**, whose love, mercy and bounty embrace all believers. Many rulers were patrons of Islam and the **ulama** — learned theologians and jurists. Like Hinduism, Islam was interpreted in a variety of ways by its followers. There were the **Shia** Muslims, who believed that the Prophet's son-in-law, **Ali**, was the legitimate leader of the Muslim community, and the **Sunni** Muslims, who accepted the authority of the early leaders (**Khalifas**) of the community and the succeeding Khalifas. There were other important differences between the various schools of law (Hanafi and Shafi'i mainly in India) and in theology and mystic traditions.

check.q: Bhakti emphasised:
options: A loving, personal relationship with a deity
check.why: Bhakti taught that devotees could reach a personal, loving god without priests or rituals.

sections.h: Thinking about time and historical periods
sections.md:
Historians do not see time just as a passing of hours, days or years — as a clock or calendar. Time also reflects changes in social and economic organisation, and in the persistence and transformation of ideas and beliefs. Dividing the past into large segments — **periods** — that possess shared characteristics makes the study of time somewhat easier.

In the middle of the 19th century, British historians divided the history of India into three periods: **"Hindu", "Muslim" and "British"**. This division (associated with **James Mill**) was based on the idea that the **religion of rulers was the only important historical change**, and that there were no other significant developments in the economy, society or culture. Such a division also **ignored the rich diversity** of the subcontinent.

Few historians follow this periodisation today. Most look to economic and social factors to characterise the major elements of different moments of the past. Histories you read in your last year included a wide range of early societies — hunter-gatherers, early farmers, people living in towns and villages, and early empires and kingdoms. The histories you will study this year are often described as **medieval**. You will find out about the spread of peasant societies, the rise of regional and imperial state formations — sometimes at the cost of pastoral and forest people — the development of Hinduism and Islam as major religions and the arrival of European trading companies.

These thousand years of Indian history witnessed considerable change. After all, the 16th and 18th centuries were quite different from the 8th or 11th. Therefore, describing the entire period as one historical unit is not without its problems. Moreover, the "medieval" period is often contrasted with the "modern" period, which carries a sense of material progress and intellectual advancement — implying the medieval period lacked change. But we know this was not the case.

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch02-new-king.title: New Kings and Kingdoms — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch02-new-king.subtitle: Samantas who became kings, the fight for Kanauj, and the mighty Cholas

sections.h: How do you become a king?
sections.md:
Imagine a powerful landlord in the Deccan around 750 CE. He commands soldiers, collects gifts from villages and serves a great king. One day he decides: why should I bow to anyone? He defeats his overlord and declares himself **maharaja-adhiraja**. That, roughly, is how many new dynasties appeared between the 7th and 12th centuries.

By the 7th century there were big landlords or warrior chiefs in different regions of the subcontinent. Existing kings often acknowledged them as their subordinates or **samantas**. They were expected to bring gifts for their kings or overlords, be present at their courts and provide them with military support. As samantas gained power and wealth, they declared themselves to be **maha-samanta, maha-mandaleshvara** (great lord of a "circle" or region) and so on. Sometimes they asserted their independence from their overlords.

**Example — the Rashtrakutas.** The Rashtrakutas in the Deccan were initially subordinate to the **Chalukyas of Karnataka**. In the mid-8th century, **Dantidurga**, a Rashtrakuta chief, overthrew his Chalukya overlord and performed a ritual called **hiranya-garbha** (literally, the golden womb). When this ritual was performed with the help of Brahmanas, it was thought to lead to the "rebirth" of the sacrificer as a Kshatriya, even if he was not one by birth.

In other cases, men from enterprising families used their **military skills** to carve out kingdoms. For instance, the **Kadamba Mayurasharman** and the **Gurjara-Pratihara Harichandra** were Brahmanas who gave up their traditional professions and took to arms, successfully establishing kingdoms in Karnataka and Rajasthan respectively.

sections.md:
Many of these new kings adopted **high-sounding titles** such as **maharaja-adhiraja** (great king, overlord of kings), **tribhuvana-chakravartin** (lord of the three worlds) and so on. However, in spite of such claims, they often **shared power** with their samantas as well as with associations of peasants, traders and Brahmanas.

In each of these states, resources were obtained from the **producers** — peasants, cattle-keepers, artisans — who were often persuaded or compelled to surrender part of what they produced. Sometimes these were claimed as **"rent"** due to a lord who asserted he owned the land. Revenue was also collected from **traders**.

These resources were used to finance the king's establishment, as well as for the construction of temples and forts. They were also used to fight wars, which were in turn expected to lead to the acquisition of wealth in the form of plunder and access to land and trade routes.

The functionaries for collecting revenue were generally recruited from **influential families**, and positions were often **hereditary**. This was true of the army as well. In many cases, close relatives of the king held these positions. **Did you know?** Inscriptions mention more than 400 different terms for taxes, including **vetti** — forced labour — and taxes on thatching the house, on climbing palm trees, on succession to family property!

check.q: Revenue in these kingdoms came mainly from:
options: Producers like peasants, cattle-keepers and artisans, and traders
check.why: Kings collected part of what producers made, plus revenue from traders.

sections.md:
**Prashastis** contain details that may not be literally true. But they tell us how rulers wanted to depict themselves — as valiant, victorious warriors, for example. These were composed by **learned Brahmanas**, who occasionally helped in administration.

A prashasti of **Nagabhata**, a Gurjara-Pratihara ruler, describes him in grand terms: he is said to have defeated the kings of Andhra, Saindhava (Sindh), Vidarbha (Maharashtra) and Kalinga (Odisha) — and then the king of Kanauj, and of Anarta (Gujarat), Malava, Kirata (forest peoples), Turushka (Turks), Vatsa and Matsya. Historians treat such lists with caution.

Kings often rewarded Brahmanas with **grants of land**. These were recorded on **copper plates**, which were given to those who received the land.

**Kalhana's Rajatarangini.** Unusually for the time, there were attempts to record histories. In the 12th century, **Kalhana** wrote a long Sanskrit poem on the history of kings who ruled over **Kashmir**. He used a variety of sources, including inscriptions, documents, eyewitness accounts and earlier histories. Unlike the writers of prashastis, he was often **critical** of rulers and their policies.

check.q: Kalhana's Rajatarangini was different from prashastis because it:
check.why: Kalhana used varied sources and did not hesitate to criticise rulers.

sections.h: Warfare for wealth: the tripartite struggle
sections.md:
Each of these ruling dynasties was based in a particular region. At the same time they tried to control other areas. One particularly prized area was the city of **Kanauj** in the Ganga valley. For centuries, rulers belonging to the **Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta and Pala** dynasties fought for control over Kanauj. Because there were three "parties" in this long-drawn conflict, historians often describe it as the **"tripartite struggle"**.

As we saw, rulers also tried to demonstrate their power and resources by building **large temples**. So when they attacked one another's kingdoms, they often chose to target temples, which were sometimes extremely rich.

**Mahmud of Ghazni.** One of the best-known such rulers was Sultan **Mahmud of Ghazni**, Afghanistan. He ruled from **997 to 1030** and extended control over parts of Central Asia, Iran and the north-western part of the subcontinent. He raided the subcontinent almost every year — his targets were wealthy temples, including that of **Somnath** in Gujarat. Much of the wealth Mahmud carried away was used to create a splendid capital city at Ghazni.

Mahmud was also interested in finding out more about the people he conquered. He entrusted a scholar named **al-Biruni** with writing an account of the subcontinent. This Arabic work, known as the **Kitab al-Hind**, remains an important source for historians. He consulted Sanskrit scholars to prepare it.

**The Chahamanas (Chauhans).** Other kings who engaged in warfare included the Chahamanas, later known as the Chauhans, who ruled over the region around **Delhi and Ajmer**. They attempted to expand their control to the west and the east, where they were opposed by the Chalukyas of Gujarat and the Gahadavalas of western Uttar Pradesh. The best-known Chahamana ruler was **Prithviraja III** (1168–1192), who defeated an Afghan ruler named **Sultan Muhammad Ghori** in **1191**, but lost to him the very next year, in **1192**.

sections.h: The Cholas: from Uraiyur to Thanjavur
sections.md:
How did the Cholas rise to power? A minor chiefly family known as the **Muttaraiyar** held power in the **Kaveri delta**. They were subordinates to the Pallava kings of Kanchipuram. **Vijayalaya**, who belonged to the ancient chiefly family of the Cholas from Uraiyur, captured the delta from the Muttaraiyar in the **middle of the 9th century**. He built the town of **Thanjavur** and a temple for goddess **Nishumbhasudini** there.

The successors of Vijayalaya conquered neighbouring regions and the kingdom grew in size and power. The Pandyan and the Pallava territories to the south and north were made part of this kingdom.

**Rajaraja I**, considered the most powerful Chola ruler, became king in **985** and expanded control over most of these areas. He also reorganised the administration of the empire. Rajaraja's son **Rajendra I** continued his policies and even raided the **Ganga valley, Sri Lanka and countries of Southeast Asia**, developing a **navy** for these expeditions.

sections.md:
The big temples of **Thanjavur** (the Rajarajeshvara or Brihadeshvara temple built by Rajaraja) and **Gangaikonda-cholapuram** (built by Rajendra I) are architectural and sculptural marvels.

Chola temples often became the **nuclei of settlements** which grew around them. These were centres of **craft production**. Temples were also endowed with land by rulers as well as by others. The produce of this land went to maintain all the specialists who worked at the temple and very often lived near it — **priests, garland makers, cooks, sweepers, musicians, dancers** etc. In other words, temples were not only places of worship; they were the hub of economic, social and cultural life as well.

Amongst the crafts associated with temples, the making of **bronze images** was the most distinctive. Chola bronze images are considered amongst the finest in the world. While most images were of deities, sometimes images were made of devotees as well. They were made using the **lost-wax technique**: a wax image is covered with clay, heated so the wax melts out, and molten bronze is poured into the hollow mould.

check.q: Chola temples were:
options: Hubs of economic, social and cultural life
check.why: Settlements, crafts and many specialists grew around temples, which held endowed land.

sections.md:
Many of the achievements of the Cholas were made possible through new developments in agriculture. The river **Kaveri** branches off into several small channels before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. These channels overflow frequently, depositing fertile soil on their banks. Water from the channels also provides the necessary moisture for agriculture, particularly the cultivation of **rice**.

Although agriculture had developed earlier in other parts of Tamil Nadu, it was only from the 5th or 6th century that this area was opened up for large-scale cultivation. Forests had to be cleared in some regions; land had to be levelled in others. In the delta region, **embankments** had to be built to prevent flooding and **canals** had to be constructed to carry water to the fields. In many areas **two crops** were grown in a year.

In many cases it was necessary to water crops artificially. A variety of methods were used for irrigation: in some areas **wells** were dug; in other places **huge tanks** were constructed to collect rainwater. Irrigation works require planning — organising labour and resources, maintaining these works and deciding on how water was to be shared. Most of the new rulers, as well as people living in villages, took an active interest in these activities.

check.q: Which river's delta was the heart of Chola agriculture?
check.why: Fertile channels of the Kaveri delta supported large-scale rice cultivation.

sections.md:
How was the administration organised? Settlements of peasants, known as **ur**, became prosperous with the spread of irrigation agriculture. Groups of such villages formed larger units called **nadu**. The village council and the nadu performed several administrative functions including dispensing justice and collecting taxes.

Rich peasants of the **Vellala** caste exercised considerable control over the affairs of the nadu under the supervision of the central Chola government. The Chola kings gave some rich landowners titles like **muvendavelan** (a velan or peasant serving three kings), **araiyar** (chief) etc. as markers of respect, and entrusted them with important offices of the state at the centre.

We have seen that Brahmanas often received land grants or **brahmadeya**. As a result, a large number of Brahmana settlements emerged in the Kaveri valley as in other parts of south India. Each brahmadeya was looked after by an **assembly or sabha** of prominent Brahmana landholders. These assemblies worked very efficiently. Their decisions were recorded in detail in inscriptions, often on the stone walls of temples. Associations of traders known as **nagarams** also occasionally performed administrative functions in towns.

**Inscriptions from Uttaramerur** in Chingleput district, Tamil Nadu, provide details of the way the sabha was organised. It had separate committees to look after irrigation works, gardens, temples etc. Names of those eligible to be members were written on small tickets of palm leaf; these tickets were put into an earthenware pot, from which a young boy was asked to take out the tickets, one by one, for each committee. Rules said members should own land from which revenue is collected, have their own homes, be between 35 and 70 years old, have knowledge of the Vedas, be well-versed in administrative matters and honest. Anyone who had been a member in the last three years could not be a member of another committee; anyone who had not submitted accounts, nor those of relatives, could not contest.

**Categories of land** in Chola inscriptions: **vellanvagai** — land of non-Brahmana peasant proprietors; **brahmadeya** — land gifted to Brahmanas; **shalabhoga** — land for the maintenance of a school; **devadana, tirunamattukkani** — land gifted to temples; **pallichchhandam** — land donated to Jaina institutions.

**Did you know?** A 13th-century Tamil text, *Periyapuranam*, describes a settlement of agricultural labourers (Pulaiyas) with small huts — a reminder that while landowners prospered, many workers lived simply. Historians also note that Uttaramerur's rules shut out most people from the sabha — it was not a democracy in our sense.

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch03-delhi-su.title: The Delhi Sultans — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch03-delhi-su.subtitle: From garrison town to empire: Raziyya, Alauddin, Muhammad Tughluq and the Mongol threat

sections.md:
Walk through Mehrauli in south Delhi today and you pass the Qutb Minar, ruined walls and old mosques — the bones of seven "cities" built over centuries. But Delhi was not always important.

Delhi first became the capital of a kingdom under the **Tomara Rajputs**, who were defeated in the middle of the 12th century by the **Chauhans** (also called Chahamanas) of Ajmer. It was under the Tomaras and Chauhans that Delhi became an important commercial centre. Many rich **Jaina merchants** lived in the city and constructed several temples. Coins minted here, called **dehliwal**, had a wide circulation.

The transformation of Delhi into a capital that controlled vast areas of the subcontinent started with the foundation of the **Delhi Sultanate** in the beginning of the **13th century**.

Period
Key rulers
rows: Qutbuddin Aybak (1206–1210), Shamsuddin Iltutmish (1210–1236), Raziyya (1236–1240), Ghiyasuddin Balban (1266–1287)

check.q: Coins minted in Delhi under the Tomaras and Chauhans were called:
check.why: Dehliwal coins from Delhi circulated widely, showing its commercial importance.

sections.h: Finding out about the Delhi Sultans
sections.md:
Although inscriptions, coins and architecture provide a lot of information, especially valuable are **histories, tarikh** (singular) / **tawarikh** (plural), written in **Persian**, the language of administration under the Delhi Sultans.

The authors of tawarikh were **learned men**: secretaries, administrators, poets and courtiers, who both recounted events and advised rulers on governance, emphasising the importance of just rule.

Keep in mind:
1. The authors of tawarikh lived in **cities** (mainly Delhi) and hardly ever in villages.
2. They often wrote their histories for Sultans in the **hope of rich rewards**.
3. These authors advised rulers on the need to preserve an "ideal" social order based on **birthright and gender distinctions**. Their ideas were not shared by everybody.

**The circle of justice** (an idea from the chronicler Fakhr-i Mudabbir, 13th century): a king can't survive without soldiers; soldiers can't live without salaries; salaries come from the revenue collected from peasants; but peasants can pay revenue only when they are prosperous and happy — which happens when the king promotes justice and honest governance.

check.q: Tawarikh were written in:
check.why: Persian was the language of administration and of the Sultanate histories.

sections.h: Raziyya: a queen on the throne
sections.md:
In **1236**, Sultan Iltutmish's daughter, **Raziyya**, became Sultan. The chronicler of the age, **Minhaj-i Siraj**, recognised that she was more able and qualified than all her brothers. But he was not comfortable at having a queen as ruler. Nor were the nobles happy at her attempts to rule independently. She was removed from the throne in **1240**.

Minhaj's discomfort shows how the ideas of the chroniclers about the "ideal" social order — where women were subordinate to men — shaped their writing.

**Did you know?** Raziyya's coins describe her proudly as the daughter of Iltutmish. Centuries later in the Deccan, **Rudramadevi** (1262–1289), of the Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal, changed her name on her inscriptions and pretended she was a man. Another queen, **Didda**, ruled in Kashmir (980–1003). Her title came from "didi" or elder sister.

check.q: Why was Minhaj-i Siraj uncomfortable with Raziyya as ruler?
options: She was a woman, which went against his idea of the social order
check.why: Though he admitted her ability, his belief that women should be subordinate made him uneasy.

sections.h: From garrison town to empire: expansion
sections.md:
In the early 13th century, the control of the Delhi Sultans rarely went beyond **heavily fortified towns occupied by garrisons**. The Sultans seldom controlled the **hinterland** of the cities and were therefore dependent upon trade, tribute or plunder for supplies.

Controlling garrison towns in distant Bengal and Sindh from Delhi was extremely difficult. Rebellion, war, even bad weather could snap fragile communication routes. The state was also challenged by **Mongol** invasions from Afghanistan and by governors who rebelled at any sign of the Sultan's weakness. The Sultanate barely survived these challenges.

Its expansion occurred during the reigns of **Ghiyasuddin Balban, Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq**.

**Internal frontier:** The first set of campaigns consolidated the **hinterlands** of the garrison towns. During these campaigns forests were cleared in the Ganga–Yamuna doab, and hunter-gatherers and pastoralists were expelled from their habitat. These lands were given to peasants and agriculture was encouraged. New fortresses, garrison towns and towns were established to protect trade routes and to promote regional trade.

**External frontier:** The second expansion occurred along the external frontier. Military expeditions into **southern India** started during the reign of Alauddin Khalji and culminated with Muhammad Tughluq. In their campaigns, Sultanate armies captured elephants, horses and slaves and carried away precious metals. By the end of Muhammad Tughluq's reign, 150 years after the Sultanate's beginnings, the armies of the Delhi Sultanate had marched across a large part of the subcontinent. They had defeated rival armies and seized cities.

check.q: Consolidating the hinterlands of garrison towns is called expansion along the:
check.why: Campaigns to control nearby hinterlands — clearing forests and settling peasants — formed the internal frontier.

sections.md:
In the Sultanate period, rulers built many **mosques** in cities all over the subcontinent. A mosque is called a **masjid** in Arabic, literally a place where a Muslim prostrates in reverence to Allah. In a "congregational mosque" (**masjid-i jami** or **jama masjid**) Muslims read their prayers (**namaz**) together. Members of the congregation choose the most respected, learned male as their leader (**imam**) for the rituals of prayer. He also delivers the sermon (**khutba**) during the Friday prayer. During prayer, Muslims stand facing **Mecca**; in India this is to the west — called the **qibla**.

The Delhi Sultans built several mosques in cities all over the subcontinent. This demonstrated their claims to be **protectors of Islam and Muslims**. Mosques also helped create the sense of a community of believers who shared a belief system and a code of conduct.

**Examples:** The **Quwwat al-Islam** mosque in Delhi, built in the late 12th century, was enlarged by Iltutmish and Alauddin. The **Qutb Minar** was started by Qutbuddin Aybak and completed by Iltutmish. The **Begumpuri mosque** was built in the reign of Muhammad Tughluq, the main mosque of Jahanpanah, his new capital in Delhi.

check.q: In India, Muslims pray facing west because:
options: Mecca lies to the west; this direction is the qibla
check.why: Muslims face Mecca in prayer, which from India lies to the west.

sections.h: Administration and consolidation: bandagan and iqtas
sections.md:
The consolidation of a kingdom as vast as the Delhi Sultanate needed reliable governors and administrators. Rather than appointing aristocrats and landed chieftains as governors, the early Delhi Sultans, especially Iltutmish, favoured their **special slaves purchased for military service**, called **bandagan** in Persian. They were carefully trained to man some of the most important political offices in the kingdom. Since they were totally dependent upon their master, the Sultan could trust and rely upon them.

The Khaljis and Tughluqs continued to use bandagan and also raised people of **humble birth**, who were often their clients, to high political positions. They were appointed as generals and governors. However, this also introduced an element of political instability. Slaves and clients were loyal to their masters and patrons, but not to their heirs. New Sultans had their own servants. As a result, the accession of a new monarch often saw conflict between the old and the new nobility. The patronage of these humble people by the Delhi Sultans also shocked many elites, and the authors of Persian tawarikh criticised the Delhi Sultans for appointing the "low and base-born" to high offices.

**Iqtas.** Like the earlier Sultans, the Khalji and Tughluq monarchs appointed military commanders as governors of territories of varying sizes. These lands were called **iqta** and their holder was called **iqtadar** or **muqti**. The duty of the muqtis was to lead military campaigns and maintain law and order in their iqtas. In exchange for their military services, the muqtis collected the revenues of their assignments as salary. They also paid their soldiers from these revenues.

Control over muqtis was most effective if their office was **not inheritable** and if they were assigned iqtas for a short period of time before being shifted. These harsh conditions of service were rigorously imposed during the reigns of Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq. **Accountants** were appointed by the state to check the amount of revenue collected by the muqtis. Care was taken that the muqti collected only the taxes prescribed by the state and that he kept the required number of soldiers.
keyTerms: Bandagan — specially trained military slaves
Iqta — territory assigned to a commander
Muqti / iqtadar — holder of an iqta

check.q: Why were muqtis shifted between iqtas frequently?
options: To prevent them from building hereditary local power
check.why: Short, non-inheritable assignments kept muqtis dependent on the Sultan.

sections.md:
As the Delhi Sultans brought the hinterland of the cities under their control, they forced the landed chieftains — the **samanta** aristocrats — and rich landlords to accept their authority. Under Alauddin Khalji the state brought the assessment and collection of land revenue under its own control. The rights of the local chieftains to levy taxes were cancelled and they were also forced to pay taxes.

The Sultan's administrators measured the land and kept careful accounts. Some of the old chieftains and landlords served the Sultanate as revenue collectors and assessors. There were **three types of taxes**:
1. on **cultivation**, called **kharaj**, amounting to about **50 per cent** of the peasant's produce;
2. on **cattle**;
3. on **houses**.

It is important to remember that large parts of the subcontinent remained **outside the control** of the Delhi Sultans. It was difficult to control distant provinces like Bengal from Delhi, and soon after annexing southern India, the entire region became independent. Even in the Gangetic plain there were forested areas that Sultanate forces could not penetrate. Local chieftains established their rule in these regions. Sometimes rulers like Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq could force their control in these areas, but only for a short duration.

**Ibn Battuta's story.** The traveller **Ibn Battuta**, from Morocco, came to Delhi in the 14th century during Muhammad Tughluq's reign. He described how chieftains fortified themselves in mountains, rocky and uneven places, as well as in bamboo groves, which were impenetrable, and how travellers were often attacked on the roads.

check.q: Kharaj was a tax on:
check.why: Kharaj was the land-revenue tax on cultivation, roughly 50 per cent of produce.

sections.h: The Mongol challenge: Alauddin vs Muhammad Tughluq
sections.md: Alauddin's measures were widely praised by chroniclers for their efficiency and for keeping prices low. Muhammad Tughluq's plans were bold and imaginative but turned into disasters: the forced shift to Daulatabad was resented and later reversed, high taxes during famine caused revolts, and the token currency had to be withdrawn. Historians today see Muhammad Tughluq as an ambitious ruler whose experiments failed partly because of poor execution and bad timing.

left.title: Alauddin Khalji
points: Faced Delhi attacked twice (1299/1300 and 1302–1303) and took defensive measures
Built a new garrison town, Siri, for his soldiers
Fed soldiers through produce collected as tax from the Ganga–Yamuna doab: tax fixed at 50% of the yield
Paid soldiers in cash; to keep cost low he controlled prices of goods in Delhi; officers ensured merchants sold at fixed prices
Measures were successful: praised for cheap prices and efficient supplies; withstood the Mongol threat

right.title: Muhammad Tughluq
points: Defeated the Mongol army and was confident of his strength; planned to attack Transoxiana
Raised a large standing army; emptied the oldest of Delhi's cities (Dehli-i Kuhna) of residents and sent them to Daulatabad, the new capital in the south
Used produce from the same area for his army, but also imposed additional taxes — coinciding with famine — leading to widespread rebellion

check.q: Muhammad Tughluq's 'token' currency failed because:
options: People did not trust coins of cheap metal and they were easily forged
check.why: Cheap-metal tokens lacked intrinsic value, so people distrusted them and forgeries flooded the market.

sections.h: The Sultanate in the 15th and 16th centuries
sections.md:
After the Tughluqs, the **Sayyid** and **Lodi** dynasties ruled from Delhi and Agra until **1526**. By then, **Jaunpur, Bengal, Malwa, Gujarat, Rajasthan** and the entire south India had independent rulers who established flourishing states and prosperous capitals. This was also the period which saw the emergence of new ruling groups like the **Afghans and the Rajputs**.

Some of the states established in this period were small but powerful and extremely well administered. **Sher Shah Sur** (1540–1545) started his career as the manager of a small territory for his uncle in Bihar and eventually challenged and defeated the Mughal emperor **Humayun** (1530–1540, 1555–1556). Sher Shah captured Delhi and established his own dynasty. Although the **Sur dynasty** ruled for only fifteen years (1540–1555), it introduced an administration that borrowed elements from Alauddin Khalji and made them more efficient. Sher Shah's administration became the model followed by the great emperor **Akbar** (1556–1605) when he consolidated the Mughal Empire.

fig.caption: Delhi Sultanate timeline.

check.q: Whose administration became a model for Akbar?
check.why: Sher Shah refined earlier systems, and Akbar followed his efficient administration.

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch04-mughal-e.title: The Mughal Empire — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch04-mughal-e.subtitle: Babur to Aurangzeb: battles and alliances, mansabdars and jagirs, zabt and sulh-i kul — how one dynasty ruled most of the subcontinent.

sections.h: An empire too big to rule — yet ruled
sections.md:
Ruling a land as vast and diverse as the Indian subcontinent was extremely difficult for medieval rulers. Yet from the latter half of the sixteenth century, the **Mughals** expanded their kingdom from Agra and Delhi until, in the seventeenth century, they controlled nearly **all of the subcontinent**. They imposed structures of administration and ideas of governance that outlasted their rule, leaving a political legacy that later rulers could not ignore.

**Who were the Mughals?** They were descendants of two great lineages of rulers. From their **mother's side** they were descendants of **Genghis Khan** (died 1227), the Mongol ruler who ruled over parts of China and Central Asia. From their **father's side** they were successors of **Timur** (died 1404), the ruler of Iran, Iraq and modern-day Turkey. However, the Mughals did not like to be called *Mughal* or *Mongol*, because Genghis Khan's memory was associated with the massacre of innumerable people. They were proud of their **Timurid** ancestry, not least because their great ancestor had captured Delhi in 1398.

check.q: Why did the Mughals prefer to be called Timurids?
options: Genghis Khan's memory was linked with massacres, and they were proud of Timur's capture of Delhi
check.why: They avoided association with Genghis Khan's violence and celebrated Timur, who had captured Delhi in 1398.

sections.md:
**Babur** (1526–1530), the first Mughal emperor, succeeded to the throne of Ferghana in **1494** when he was only **12 years old**. He was forced to leave his ancestral throne due to the invasion of another Mongol group, the **Uzbegs**. After years of wandering he seized **Kabul in 1504**.

- **1526**: defeated the Sultan of Delhi, **Ibrahim Lodi**, at **Panipat** and captured Delhi and Agra.
- **1527**: defeated **Rana Sanga**, Rajput rulers and allies at **Khanua**.
- **1528**: defeated the Rajputs at **Chanderi**; established control over Agra and Delhi before his death.

**Humayun** (1530–1540, 1555–1556) divided his inheritance according to the will of his father; his brothers were each given a province. The ambitions of his brother **Mirza Kamran** weakened Humayun's cause against Afghan competitors.
- **Sher Khan** defeated Humayun at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kanauj (1540)**, forcing him to flee to **Iran**.
- In Iran, Humayun received help from the **Safavid Shah**.
- He recaptured **Delhi in 1555** but died the next year after an accident in this building (falling down the stairs of his library).

sections.md:
**Akbar** became emperor at **13**. His reign can be divided into three periods:

**1556–1570**: Akbar became independent of the regent **Bairam Khan** and other members of his domestic staff. Military campaigns were launched against the **Suris and other Afghans**, against the neighbouring kingdoms of **Malwa and Gondwana**, and to suppress the revolt of his half-brother Mirza Hakim and the Uzbegs. In **1568** the Sisodiya capital of **Chittor** was seized, and in **1569 Ranthambhor**.

**1570–1585**: military campaigns in **Gujarat**, followed by campaigns in the east in **Bihar, Bengal and Orissa** — complicated by the 1579–1580 revolt in support of Mirza Hakim.

**1585–1605**: expansion of Akbar's empire. Campaigns were launched in the **north-west**. **Qandahar** was seized from the Safavids, **Kashmir** was annexed, as also **Kabul** after the death of Mirza Hakim. Campaigns in the **Deccan** started and **Berar, Khandesh** and parts of **Ahmadnagar** were annexed. In the last years of his reign, Akbar's power was distracted by the rebellion of the future emperor **Jahangir**.

(The **Second Battle of Panipat, 1556**, in which the Mughals defeated **Hemu**, began Akbar's reign.)

check.q: In which year was Chittor seized by Akbar?
check.why: Akbar captured the Sisodiya capital of Chittor in 1568, followed by Ranthambhor in 1569.

sections.md:
**Jahangir (1605–1627)** continued the military campaigns started by Akbar. The Sisodiya ruler of Mewar, **Amar Singh**, accepted Mughal service. Less successful campaigns were launched against the Sikhs, the Ahoms and Ahmadnagar. Prince **Khurram**, the future Shah Jahan, rebelled in the last years of his reign. The efforts of Jahangir's wife, **Nur Jahan**, to marginalise him were unsuccessful.

**Shah Jahan (1627–1658)** continued Mughal campaigns in the **Deccan**. The Afghan noble **Khan Jahan Lodi** rebelled and was defeated. Campaigns were launched against **Ahmadnagar**; the Bundelas were defeated and Orchha seized. In the north-west, the campaign to seize **Balkh** from the Uzbegs was unsuccessful and Qandahar was lost to the Safavids. In **1632 Ahmadnagar was finally annexed** and the Bijapur forces sued for peace. In 1657–1658, there was conflict over succession amongst his sons. **Aurangzeb** was victorious and his three brothers, including **Dara Shukoh**, were killed. Shah Jahan was imprisoned for the rest of his life in Agra.

**Aurangzeb (1658–1707)**: In the north-east, the **Ahoms were defeated in 1663**, but rebelled again in the 1680s. Campaigns in the north-west against the Yusufzai and the Sikhs were temporarily successful. Mughal intervention in the succession and internal politics of the Rathor Rajputs of Marwar led to their rebellion. Campaigns against the Maratha chieftain **Shivaji** were initially successful. But Aurangzeb insulted Shivaji, who escaped from Agra, declared himself an independent king and resumed his campaigns against the Mughals. Prince **Akbar** rebelled against Aurangzeb and received support from the Marathas and Deccan Sultanate; he finally fled to Safavid Iran. After Akbar's rebellion Aurangzeb sent armies against the Deccan Sultanates. **Bijapur was annexed in 1685 and Golconda in 1687**. From 1698 Aurangzeb personally managed campaigns in the Deccan against the Marathas, who started guerrilla warfare. Aurangzeb also had to face the rebellion in north India of the **Sikhs, Jats and Satnamis**, in the north-east of the Ahoms and in the Deccan of the Marathas. His death was followed by a succession conflict amongst his sons.

sections.h: Succession and relations with other rulers
sections.md:
**Succession**: The Mughals did not believe in the rule of **primogeniture**, where the eldest son inherited his father's estate. Instead they followed the Mughal and Timurid custom of **coparcenary inheritance**, or a division of the inheritance amongst all the sons. This often led to wars of succession among princes.

**Relations with other rulers**: Mughal rulers campaigned constantly against rulers who refused to accept their authority. But as the Mughals became powerful, many other rulers also joined them **voluntarily**. The **Rajputs** are a good example. Many of them married their daughters into Mughal families and received high positions. Many resisted as well.

- The mother of **Jahangir** was a **Kachhwaha princess**, daughter of the Rajput ruler of **Amber** (modern-day Jaipur).
- The mother of **Shah Jahan** was a **Rathor princess**, daughter of the Rajput ruler of **Marwar** (Jodhpur).

The **Sisodiya Rajputs** refused to accept Mughal authority for a long time. Once defeated, however, they were honourably treated by the Mughals, given their lands (*watan*) back as assignments (*watan jagir*). The careful balance between defeating but not humiliating their opponents enabled the Mughals to extend their influence over many kings and chieftains. But it was difficult to keep this balance all the time.
keyTerms: primogeniture — eldest son inherits everything
coparcenary — inheritance shared among all sons
watan jagir — a ruler's homeland returned as a Mughal assignment

check.q: What was coparcenary inheritance?
options: Inheritance was divided among all sons
check.why: Following Timurid custom, all sons had a claim to inheritance, which often caused succession wars.

sections.md:
As the empire expanded to encompass different regions, the Mughals recruited diverse bodies of people. From a small nucleus of **Turkish nobles (Turanis)**, they expanded to include **Iranians, Indian Muslims, Afghans, Rajputs, Marathas** and other groups. Those who joined Mughal service were enrolled as **mansabdars**.

The term *mansabdar* refers to an individual who holds a **mansab**, meaning a **position or rank**. It was a grading system used by the Mughals to fix (1) rank, (2) salary and (3) military responsibilities. Rank and salary were determined by a numerical value called **zat**. The higher the zat, the more prestigious was the noble's position in court and the larger his salary.

The mansabdar's military responsibilities required him to maintain a specified number of **sawar** or cavalrymen. The mansabdar brought his cavalrymen for review, got them registered, their horses branded and then received money to pay them as salary.

Mansabdars received their salaries as revenue assignments called **jagirs**, which were somewhat like iqtas. But unlike muqtis, most mansabdars did not actually reside in or administer their jagirs. They only had rights to the revenue, which was collected for them by their servants while the mansabdars themselves served in some other part of the country.

In **Akbar's** reign, jagirs were carefully assessed so that their revenues were roughly equal to the salary of the mansabdar. By **Aurangzeb's** reign this was no longer the case, and the actual revenue collected was often less than the granted sum. There was also a huge increase in the number of mansabdars, which meant a long wait before they received a jagir. These and other factors created a shortage of jagirs. As a result, many jagirdars tried to extract as much revenue as possible while they had a jagir. Aurangzeb was unable to control these developments in the last years of his reign, and peasants suffered tremendously.

sections.md:
The main source of income available to Mughal rulers was **tax on the produce of the peasantry**. In most places, peasants paid taxes through the rural elites — the headman or the local chieftain. The Mughals used one term — **zamindars** — to describe all intermediaries, whether they were local headmen of villages or powerful chieftains.

Akbar's revenue minister, **Todar Mal**, carried out a careful survey of crop yields, prices and areas cultivated for a **10-year period, 1570–1580**. On the basis of this data, tax was fixed **on each crop in cash**. Each province was divided into revenue circles with its own schedule of revenue rates for individual crops. This revenue system was known as **zabt**. It was prevalent in those areas where Mughal administrators could survey the land and keep very careful accounts. This was not possible in provinces such as Gujarat and Bengal.

In some areas the zamindars exercised a great deal of power. The exploitation by Mughal administrators could drive them to rebellion. Sometimes zamindars and peasants of the same caste allied in rebelling against Mughal authority. These peasant revolts challenged the stability of the Mughal Empire from the end of the seventeenth century.

check.q: Who carried out the crop survey on which zabt was based?
check.why: Akbar's revenue minister Todar Mal surveyed yields and prices over 1570–1580 to fix cash revenue rates.

sections.md:
**Abul Fazl**, Akbar's friend and courtier, wrote a three-volume history of Akbar's reign titled ***Akbar Nama***. The first volume dealt with Akbar's ancestors, the second recorded events of his reign, and the third, the ***Ain-i Akbari***, dealt with his administration, household, army, revenues and the geography of his empire. It also provides rich details about the traditions and culture of the people living in India — with statistical details about crops, yields, prices, wages and revenues.

While Akbar was at **Fatehpur Sikri** during the **1570s** he started discussions on religion with the ulama, Brahmanas, Jesuit priests who were Roman Catholics, and Zoroastrians. These discussions took place in the **ibadat khana**. He was interested in the religion and social customs of different people. It made him realise that religious scholars who emphasised ritual and dogma were often bigots. Their teachings created divisions and disharmony amongst his subjects. This eventually led Akbar to the idea of **sulh-i kul** or **'universal peace'**.

This idea of tolerance did not discriminate between people of different religions in his realm. Instead it focused on a system of ethics — honesty, justice, peace — that was universally applicable. Abul Fazl helped Akbar in framing a vision of governance around this idea. This principle of governance was followed by **Jahangir and Shah Jahan** as well.

**The empire in the 17th century and after**: The administrative and military efficiency of the Mughal Empire led to great economic and commercial prosperity. International travellers described it as the fabled land of wealth. But the same travellers were also appalled at the state of poverty that existed side by side with the greatest opulence. The inequalities were glaring. As the authority of the Mughal emperor slowly declined, his servants emerged as powerful centres in the regions. They constituted new dynasties and held command of provinces like **Hyderabad and Awadh**. Although they continued to recognise the Mughal emperor in Delhi as their master, by the eighteenth century the provinces of the empire had consolidated their independent political identities.

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch05-tribes-n.title: Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch05-tribes-n.subtitle: Beyond the big cities: Banjara caravans, the Gond kingdoms and the Ahoms of Assam

sections.md:
So far in this book we have met Sultans in Delhi, Chola kings in Thanjavur and grand temples. But most people of the subcontinent lived somewhere else: in villages, forests, hills and grasslands. What was life like there?

In large parts of the subcontinent, society was already divided according to the rules of **varna**. These rules, as prescribed by the Brahmanas, were accepted by the rulers of large kingdoms. The difference between high and low, and between rich and poor, increased. Under the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, this hierarchy between social classes grew further.

However, there were other kinds of societies as well. Many societies in the subcontinent **did not follow the social rules and rituals prescribed by the Brahmanas**. Nor were they divided into numerous unequal classes. Such societies are often called **tribes**.

check.q: Tribal societies generally:
options: Did not follow Brahmanical rules and were not divided into many unequal classes
check.why: Tribes stood outside varna rules and were less divided into unequal classes.

sections.md:
Members of each tribe were united by **kinship bonds**. Many tribes obtained their livelihood from **agriculture**. Others were **hunter-gatherers or herders**. Most often they combined these activities to make full use of the natural resources of the area in which they lived. Some tribes were **nomadic** and moved from one place to another. A tribal group controlled land and pastures jointly, and divided these amongst households according to its own rules.

Many large tribes thrived in **forests, hills, deserts** and places difficult to reach. Sometimes they clashed with the more powerful caste-based societies. In various ways, the tribes retained their freedom and preserved their separate culture. But the caste-based and tribal societies also depended on each other for their diverse needs. This relationship, of conflict and dependence, gradually caused both societies to change.

**How do we know?** Contemporary historians and travellers give very scanty information about tribes. A few exceptions apart, tribal people **did not keep written records**. But they preserved rich customs and **oral traditions**, passed down to each new generation. Present-day historians have started using such oral traditions to write tribal histories.

sections.md:
Some tribes became powerful and controlled large territories. In **Punjab**, the **Khokhar** tribe was very influential during the 13th and 14th centuries. Later, the **Gakkhars** became more important; their chief, **Kamal Khan Gakkhar**, was made a noble (**mansabdar**) by Emperor Akbar. In **Multan and Sind**, the **Langahs and Arghuns** dominated extensive regions before they were subdued by the Mughals. The **Balochis** were another large and powerful tribe in the north-west, divided into many smaller clans under different chiefs.

In the western Himalaya lived the shepherd tribe of **Gaddis**. The distant north-eastern part of the subcontinent too was entirely dominated by tribes — the **Nagas, Ahoms** and many others.

In many areas of present-day **Bihar and Jharkhand**, **Chero** chiefdoms had emerged by the 12th century. Raja Man Singh, Akbar's famous general, attacked and defeated the Cheros in 1591. A large amount of booty was taken from them, but they were not entirely subdued. Under Aurangzeb, Mughal forces captured many Chero fortresses and subjugated the tribe. The **Mundas and Santals** were among the other important tribes that lived in this region and also in Odisha and Bengal.

The Maharashtra highlands and Karnataka were home to **Kolis, Berads** and numerous others. Kolis also lived in many areas of Gujarat. Further south there were large tribal populations of **Koragas, Vetars, Maravars** and many others. The large tribe of **Bhils** was spread across western and central India. By the late 16th century, many of them had become settled agriculturists and some even zamindars. Many Bhil clans, nevertheless, remained hunter-gatherers. The **Gonds** were found in great numbers across the present-day states of Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.

check.q: Which Gakkhar chief became a mansabdar under Akbar?
check.why: Akbar made Kamal Khan Gakkhar a noble, showing how tribes joined Mughal politics.

sections.h: How nomads and mobile people lived
sections.md:
**Nomadic pastoralists** moved over long distances with their animals. They lived on milk and other pastoral products. They also exchanged wool, ghee etc. with settled agriculturists for grain, cloth, utensils and other products. They bought and sold these goods as they moved from one place to another, transporting them on their animals.

**The Banjaras** were the most important trader-nomads. Their caravan was called a **tanda**. **Sultan Alauddin Khalji** used the Banjaras to transport grain to the city markets. Emperor **Jahangir** wrote in his memoirs that the Banjaras carried grain on their bullocks from different areas and sold it in towns. They transported food grain for the Mughal army during military campaigns. With a large army there could be 1,00,000 bullocks carrying grain.

A 17th-century European traveller, **Peter Mundy**, described meeting a Banjara tanda of about **14,000 oxen** carrying grain such as wheat and rice; they took their wives and children with them, and the caravans were led by a chief called the *naik*.

Many pastoral tribes reared and sold animals, such as **cattle and horses**, to the prosperous people. Different castes of **petty pedlars** also travelled from village to village. They manufactured and sold wares such as ropes, reeds, straw matting and coarse sacks. Sometimes **mendicants** acted as wandering merchants. There were castes of **entertainers** who performed in different towns and villages for their livelihood.

sections.h: Changing society: new castes and hierarchies
sections.md:
As the economy and the needs of society grew, people with new skills were required. Smaller castes, or **jatis**, emerged within varnas. For example, new castes emerged amongst the Brahmanas. On the other hand, many tribes and social groups were taken into caste-based society and given the status of jatis. Specialised **artisans** — smiths, carpenters and masons — were also recognised as separate jatis by the Brahmanas. Jatis, rather than varna, became the basis for organising society.

Among the Kshatriyas, new **Rajput clans** became powerful by the 11th and 12th centuries. They belonged to different lineages, such as the **Hunas, Chandelas, Chalukyas** and others. Some of these had been tribes earlier. Many of these clans came to be regarded as Rajputs. They gradually replaced the older rulers, especially in agricultural areas. Here a variety of changes were taking place, and rulers used their wealth to create powerful states.

The rise of Rajput clans to the position of rulers set an example for the tribal people to follow. Gradually, with the support of the Brahmanas, many tribes became part of the caste system. But only the leading tribal families could join the ruling class. A large majority joined the lower jatis of caste society. On the other hand, many dominant tribes of Punjab, Sind and the North-West Frontier had adopted **Islam** quite early. They continued to reject the caste system. The unequal social order, prescribed by orthodox Hinduism, was not widely accepted in these areas.

The emergence of states is closely related to changes in tribal societies. Two important examples of this are the **Gonds** and the **Ahoms**.

check.q: Which of these were Rajput lineages that had once been tribes?
check.why: The chapter names Hunas, Chandelas and Chalukyas among lineages that came to be regarded as Rajputs.

sections.md:
The Gonds lived in a vast forested region called **Gondwana** — "country inhabited by Gonds". They practised **shifting cultivation**. The large Gond tribe was further divided into many smaller clans. Each clan had its own raja or rai.

About the time the power of the Delhi Sultans was declining, a few large Gond kingdoms were beginning to dominate the smaller Gond chiefs. The **Akbar Nama**, a history of Akbar's reign, mentions the Gond kingdom of **Garha Katanga** that had **70,000 villages**.

**Administration.** The kingdom was divided into **garhs**. Each garh was controlled by a particular Gond clan. This was further divided into units of **84 villages** called **chaurasi**. The chaurasi was subdivided into **barhots**, made up of 12 villages each.

The emergence of large states changed the nature of Gond society. Their basically equal society gradually got divided into **unequal social classes**. Brahmanas received land grants from the Gond rajas and became more influential. The Gond chiefs now wished to be recognised as Rajputs. So **Aman Das**, the Gond raja of Garha Katanga, assumed the title of **Sangram Shah**. His son, **Dalpat**, married princess **Durgawati**, the daughter of **Salbahan**, the Chandel Rajput raja of **Mahoba**.

Dalpat, however, died early. Rani Durgawati was very capable and started ruling on behalf of her five-year-old son, **Bir Narain**. Under her, the kingdom became even more extensive. In **1565**, the Mughal forces under **Asaf Khan** attacked Garha Katanga. A strong resistance was put up by Rani Durgawati. She was defeated and preferred death to surrender. Her son too died fighting soon after.

Garha Katanga was a rich state. It earned much wealth by trapping and exporting **wild elephants** to other kingdoms. When the Mughals defeated the Gonds, they captured a huge booty of precious coins and elephants. They annexed part of the kingdom and granted the rest to **Chandra Shah**, an uncle of Bir Narain. Despite the fall of Garha Katanga, the Gond kingdoms survived for some time. However, they became much weaker and later struggled unsuccessfully against the stronger Bundelas and Marathas.

sections.md:
The **Ahoms** migrated to the **Brahmaputra valley** from present-day **Myanmar** in the **13th century**. They created a new state by suppressing the older political system of the **bhuiyans** (landlords). During the 16th century, they annexed the kingdoms of the **Chhutiyas (1523)** and of **Koch-Hajo (1581)** and subjugated many other tribes. The Ahoms built a large state, and for this they used **firearms** as early as the 1530s. By the 1660s they could even make high-quality gunpowder and cannons.

However, the Ahoms faced many invasions from the south-west. In **1662**, the Mughals under **Mir Jumla** attacked the Ahom kingdom. Despite their brave defence, the Ahoms were defeated. But direct Mughal control over the region could not last long.

**The paik system.** The Ahom state depended upon **forced labour**. Those forced to work for the state were called **paiks**. A census of the population was taken. Each village had to send a number of paiks by rotation. People from heavily populated areas were shifted to less populated places. Ahom clans were thus broken up. By the first half of the 17th century the administration became quite centralised.

Almost all adult males served in the **army** during war. At other times, they were engaged in building **dams, irrigation systems** etc. The Ahoms also introduced new methods of **rice cultivation**.

**Society.** Ahom society was divided into clans or **khels**. There were very few castes of artisans, so artisans in the Ahom areas came from the adjoining kingdoms. A khel often controlled several villages. The peasant was given land by his village community. Even the king could not take it away without the community's consent.

Originally, the Ahoms worshipped their own **tribal gods**. During the first half of the 17th century, however, the influence of Brahmanas increased. Temples and Brahmanas were granted land by the king. In the reign of **Sib Singh (1714–1744)**, Hinduism became the predominant religion. But the Ahom kings did not completely give up their traditional beliefs after adopting Hinduism.

Ahom society was very sophisticated. **Poets and scholars** were given land grants. **Theatre** was encouraged. Important works of Sanskrit were translated into the local language. Historical works, known as **buranjis**, were also written — first in the **Ahom language** and then in **Assamese**.

sections.md:
Considerable changes took place in tribal societies during this period. Some tribes became powerful and founded states (Gonds, Ahoms); others were absorbed into caste society as jatis, or took up settled farming (many Bhils). Some, like the Banjaras, connected villages, towns and armies through trade. Tribal societies interacted with the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals — sometimes fighting (Cheros, Gonds, Ahoms), sometimes joining them (Gakkhars).

At the same time, tribal people kept many of their own customs, languages, festivals and gods. Their histories, long ignored by court chroniclers, are now being recovered by historians from oral traditions, ballads, local records and the chronicles such as the buranjis. The relationship of caste and tribe — conflict and dependence — shaped the medieval subcontinent as much as the big empires did.

**Think about it:** Can you find out about a tribe living in your state today? What languages do they speak and what festivals do they celebrate?

rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch06-devotion.title: Devotional Paths to the Divine
rd-school-c7-social-a.hist-ch06-devotion.subtitle: How poets, weavers, saints and singers told India that God can be reached through love

sections.md:
Imagine Varanasi, around 1450. In a lane full of looms, a weaver pauses between threads and sings a couplet. It is short, sharp and funny. It asks why people bathe in rivers and count beads, yet keep hatred in their hearts. Passers-by laugh, then fall silent, because the question is aimed at them. The weaver is **Kabir**, and his songs are still sung across India more than five hundred years later.

This chapter is about people like Kabir — men and women who said that the divine is not locked inside temples, rituals or the rules of one caste. You could reach God, they said, through **bhakti** (loving devotion), through honest work, through remembering the divine name, and through treating every person as equal.

For centuries before this, many people had worshipped gods and goddesses through elaborate rituals, often conducted by priests. Ideas about **purity and impurity**, and about a fixed social order based on birth, had become stronger. Some thinkers such as the Buddha and Mahavira had earlier questioned this, and taught that people could seek liberation through their own effort. The idea of a **supreme God** who could free devotees from the cycle of birth and rebirth through love also slowly grew. Stories of Shiva, Vishnu and the Goddess, told in the **Puranas**, became popular, and anyone, whatever their caste, could worship with devotion.

The idea of bhakti appears clearly in the **Bhagavad Gita**, where devotion to God is praised as a path to liberation. In the centuries that followed, this idea became a mighty movement — or rather, many movements, in many languages, across the whole subcontinent.

> **Did you know?** The word *bhakti* comes from a Sanskrit root meaning 'to share' or 'to take part' — the devotee shares in the divine through love.
keyTerms: Bhakti — loving devotion to a personal god
Puranas — collections of stories about gods and goddesses
Purity/impurity — beliefs used to rank people and rituals

check.q: Which idea lies at the heart of bhakti?
options: Loving devotion can bring a person close to God
God can be reached only by people of high birth
check.why: Bhakti teaches that sincere, loving devotion — open to anyone — is the path to the divine.

sections.h: Nayanars and Alvars: the singing saints of the south
sections.md:
The bhakti movement found an early and powerful voice in Tamil Nadu between about the **seventh and ninth centuries**. Two groups of poet-saints travelled from place to place singing in Tamil:

- The **Nayanars** — devotees of **Shiva**. Tradition counts 63 Nayanars.
- The **Alvars** — devotees of **Vishnu**. Tradition counts 12 Alvars.

What made them remarkable was *who they were*. They came from all castes, including those considered 'untouchable', and included potters, farmers, hunters, soldiers, Brahmins and chiefs. Some were women. One famous Nayanar woman was **Karaikkal Ammaiyar**; a famous woman Alvar was **Andal**, whose poems express her love for Vishnu.

They sharply criticised the idea that birth decided worth. They visited sacred shrines, praised the local deity in songs, and turned the temple towns into places of pilgrimage. Their songs were later collected: the Alvars' poems in the **Divya Prabandham**, and the Nayanars' songs in the **Tevaram** and Tiruvacakam.

Between the tenth and twelfth centuries, the **Chola and Pandya kings** built grand temples around many of the shrines these saints had visited. This strengthened the bond between bhakti and temple worship. Around the same time, *hagiographies* — religious biographies of the saints — were written. Historians use these, carefully, as sources: they tell us what followers believed, even if not every miracle in them is a historical fact.

| Group | Devotees of | Number (by tradition) | Collected songs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nayanars | Shiva | 63 | Tevaram, Tiruvacakam |
| Alvars | Vishnu | 12 | Divya Prabandham |

sections.h: Philosophy and bhakti: Shankara and Ramanuja
sections.md:
Not all thinkers sang in temple courtyards. Some argued with careful logic.

**Shankara**, born in Kerala in the **eighth century**, was one of the most influential philosophers in India. He taught **Advaita** — the doctrine of the *oneness* of the individual soul and the Supreme God, which is the Ultimate Reality. He taught that **Brahman**, the only reality, was formless and without attributes. He considered the world around us an illusion or **maya**, and preached renunciation of the world and the path of knowledge to understand Brahman and attain salvation.

**Ramanuja**, born in Tamil Nadu in the **eleventh century**, was deeply influenced by the Alvars. He believed that the best means of attaining salvation was **intense devotion to Vishnu**. Vishnu, in his grace, helps the devotee attain the bliss of union with him. He propounded **Vishishtadvaita** — *qualified oneness* — in which the soul, even when united with the Supreme God, remains distinct. His ideas greatly inspired the later bhakti in north India.

| Thinker | Century | Region | Teaching | Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shankara | 8th | Kerala | Advaita (oneness) | Knowledge, renunciation |
| Ramanuja | 11th | Tamil Nadu | Vishishtadvaita (qualified oneness) | Devotion to Vishnu |

An easy way to remember: for Shankara, a drop of water that falls into the ocean *becomes* the ocean. For Ramanuja, it is like a spark close to a fire — glowing with its light, yet still a spark.

check.q: What does 'Vishishtadvaita' mean?
check.why: Ramanuja taught qualified oneness: the soul unites with God yet remains distinct.

sections.md:
In twelfth-century Karnataka, a new movement began, led by **Basavanna** and his companions such as **Allama Prabhu** and **Akkamahadevi**. Their followers were called **Virashaivas** (or Lingayats).

They argued strongly for the **equality of all human beings** and against Brahmanical ideas about caste and the treatment of women. They were also against all forms of ritual and idol worship. They expressed their thoughts in **vachanas** — short, powerful sayings in Kannada.

One famous idea in Basavanna's vachanas contrasts the rich, who build temples for Shiva, with the poor devotee who says, in effect, 'my body is the temple; my legs are pillars; my head a golden dome'. The point is bold: what stands still (a temple) can fall, but a moving, living devotee carries the divine wherever he goes.

> **Think:** Why might people who could not enter certain temples find this message thrilling?
keyTerms: Virashaiva — Shiva-devotees' movement started by Basavanna
Vachana — a short devotional saying in Kannada

check.why: Basavanna and his companions composed vachanas in Kannada.

sections.md:
From the **thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries**, Maharashtra produced a great line of saint-poets who wrote in **Marathi**: **Jnaneshwar**, **Namdev**, **Eknath** and **Tukaram**, and women such as **Sakkubai**, along with the family of **Chokhamela**, who belonged to the 'untouchable' Mahar caste.

This regional tradition focused on the **Vitthala** (a form of Vishnu) temple at **Pandharpur**, and on the idea of a personal god residing in the hearts of all people. Their songs, called **abhangs**, are still sung by lakhs of pilgrims — the *warkaris* — who walk to Pandharpur every year, singing as they go.

These saints rejected all forms of ritualism, outward display of piety and social differences based on birth. They even rejected the idea of renunciation, preferring to live with their families, earning a living like anyone else, and humbly serving fellow human beings in need. A new humanist idea emerged: bhakti lay in **sharing others' pain**. As one saying of this tradition puts it, the true devotee is the one who understands the pain of others.

> **Did you know?** The annual Pandharpur wari is among the largest walking pilgrimages in the world, and many pilgrims cover around 250 km on foot.

check.q: The Maharashtra saints were devoted mainly to which deity?
check.why: Their devotion centred on Vitthala, a form of Vishnu, at Pandharpur.

sections.md:
Several religious groups emerged in this period that **criticised the rituals** and other aspects of conventional religion and the social order, using simple, logical arguments. Among them were the **Nathpanthis, Siddhacharas and Yogis**.

They advocated **renunciation of the world**. To them, the path to salvation lay in meditation on the formless Ultimate Reality and the realisation of oneness with it. To achieve this, they recommended intense training of the mind and body through practices like **yogasanas, breathing exercises and meditation**.

These groups became particularly popular among the 'low' castes. Their criticism of conventional religion created the ground for devotional religion to become a popular force in northern India.

check.q: Which practice did the Nathpanthis and Yogis recommend?
check.why: They believed training mind and body through yoga and meditation led to realising the formless reality.

sections.md:
The saints of the bhakti movement had much in common with the **Sufis**, who had a lot of shared ideas. Sufis were **Muslim mystics**. They rejected outward religiosity and emphasised **love and devotion to God** and compassion towards all fellow human beings.

Islam propagated strict monotheism, or submission to one God. It also rejected idol worship and simplified rituals into collective prayers. At the same time, Muslim scholars developed a holy law called the **Shariat**. The Sufis often rejected the elaborate rituals and codes of behaviour demanded by Muslim religious scholars. They sought union with God much as a lover seeks the beloved, disregarding the world around them. Like the saint-poets, Sufis composed poems expressing their feelings, and a rich literature in prose, including anecdotes and fables, developed around them. Among the great Sufis of Central Asia were **Ghazzali, Rumi and Sadi**.

Sufis also believed the heart can be trained to look at the world differently. They developed elaborate methods of training under a **master (pir or shaikh)** — **zikr** (chanting of a name or sacred formula), contemplation, **sama** (singing), **raqs** (dancing), discussion of parables, and breath control.

A large number of Sufis from Central Asia settled in Hindustan from the eleventh century. This became stronger with the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, when several major Sufi centres developed. The **Chishti silsila** was among the most influential. Its great teachers included **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti** of Ajmer, **Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki** of Delhi, **Baba Farid** of Punjab, **Khwaja Nizamuddin Auliya** of Delhi and **Bandanawaz Gisudaraz** of Gulbarga.

The Sufi masters held their assemblies in their **khanqahs** (hospices). Devotees of all descriptions — members of the royal household, nobility, ordinary people — flocked there. People sought the masters' blessing and visited their tombs, or **dargahs**, which became places of pilgrimage. Even today, qawwalis echo at the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi and at Ajmer Sharif.

sections.h: New religious developments in north India: Kabir
sections.md:
After the thirteenth century, a new wave of the bhakti movement rose in north India, an age when Islam, Brahmanical Hinduism, Sufism, various strands of bhakti, and the Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis influenced one another. Some saints, like **Tulsidas** and **Surdas**, accepted existing beliefs and practices but wanted to make them accessible to all. Tulsidas conceived of God in the form of **Rama**; his composition the **Ramcharitmanas**, in Awadhi, is important both as an expression of devotion and as a literary work. Surdas was an ardent devotee of **Krishna**; his compositions are compiled in the *Sursagar, Surasaravali* and *Sahitya Lahari*. Also from this time were **Shankaradeva** of Assam (later fifteenth century), who emphasised devotion to Vishnu and composed poems and plays in Assamese, beginning the practice of setting up **namghars** (houses of recitation and prayer), and **Dadu Dayal, Ravidas and Mirabai**.

**Mirabai** was a Rajput princess married into the royal family of Mewar in the sixteenth century. She became a disciple of **Ravidas**, a saint from a caste considered 'untouchable'. She was devoted to Krishna and composed innumerable bhajans expressing her intense devotion. Her songs openly challenged the norms of the 'upper' castes and became popular with the masses in Rajasthan and Gujarat.

A unique feature of most of these saints is that their works were composed in **regional languages** and could be sung. They became immensely popular and were handed down orally from generation to generation — often by the poorest and most deprived communities and women.

**Kabir**, who probably lived in the fifteenth–sixteenth centuries, was one of the most influential saints. He was brought up in a family of Muslim **julahas** (weavers) settled in or near Benares (Varanasi). Kabir's ideas come to us from a vast collection of verses called *sakhis* and *pads*, said to have been composed by him and sung by wandering bhajan singers. Some were later collected and preserved in the **Guru Granth Sahib**, *Panch Vani* and *Bijak*.

Kabir's teachings were based on a complete, indeed vehement, **rejection of the major religious traditions**. He openly ridiculed all forms of external worship of both Brahmanical Hinduism and Islam, the pre-eminence of the priestly classes and the caste system. His poetry used a spoken form of Hindi widely understood by ordinary people, and sometimes a cryptic language difficult to follow. Kabir believed in a **formless Supreme God** and preached that the only path to salvation was through bhakti. He drew followers from among both Hindus and Muslims.
