fig.caption: A climber zig-zags to the summit — the outer climb. The essay is about the inner one.
fig.alt: Animated climber reaching a peak

sections.h: Paragraph 1: Mixed feelings at the top
sections.md:
The writer says people often ask him what he felt on top of Everest. His answer: a mixture of emotions that are hard to put in words.

- **Joy and achievement** — the goal of years was reached.
- **Humility** — he felt small before the vastness of nature, and grateful.
- **Sadness** — a strange feeling that there was nothing higher to climb; all roads now lead down.

He compares this to life: success brings joy but also a sense of 'what next?'

**Meaning:** great achievements are not just thrilling; they are deep, quiet and humbling.

check.q: Which feeling did the writer NOT describe at the summit?
options: Sadness that there was nowhere higher
check.why: He felt joy, humility and a touch of sadness — never a wish to beat others.

sections.md:
The essay asks the famous question: *why do people climb mountains?* The quick reply, 'because it is there', is not enough for Ahluwalia.

- Mountains are **nature at its best**: beautiful, grand, challenging.
- Climbing tests **endurance, persistence and will-power**.
- Overcoming danger and hardship gives a lasting **sense of achievement**.

He says the climber comes closer to nature and, in a way, closer to God. On the summit he felt deep awe — a spiritual experience.
keyTerms: Endurance — the ability to keep going through hardship
Persistence — not giving up
Exhilaration — great excitement and joy

sections.md:
Ahluwalia describes the sacred things climbers left on top:

| Climber | Offering |
|---|---|
| Rawat | a picture of Goddess Durga |
| Phu Dorji | a relic of the Buddha |
| Ahluwalia | a picture of Guru Nanak |
| Edmund Hillary (1953) | had buried a cross in the snow |

**Meaning:** at the top of the world, people of different faiths gave thanks side by side. Nature unites us; the summit is a place of humility, not conquest. The writer felt they were not 'conquering' the mountain but being allowed to stand on it.

check.q: What did Phu Dorji leave on the summit?
check.why: Phu Dorji left a relic of the Buddha, showing the shared spirit of many faiths.

sections.md:
From the top, the writer saw great peaks — Lhotse, Nuptse, Makalu — lying below, and clouds far beneath. Mountains that look enormous from the valley seemed small. He felt a strange loneliness too.

Then came the realisation that the climb down is as dangerous as the climb up. Many accidents happen on the descent, when the body is tired and the mind relaxes. The summit is not the end.

**Meaning:** after success, stay humble and careful.

Here is the heart of the essay. Climbing Everest is a **physical** climb, but there is another climb that is **emotional** and **spiritual**: overcoming fear, anger, jealousy, laziness and selfishness in ourselves.

That inner mountain is just as high and as hard. It needs the same qualities: endurance, persistence, will-power. Ahluwalia says the climb of the 'summit within' is as satisfying as — even more than — the physical one.

**Meaning:** every person faces an inner Everest. When you control a bad temper, keep studying after failing, or forgive a friend, you are climbing your summit within.

check.q: What is 'the summit within'?
check.why: It is the inner climb — conquering fear, anger and other weaknesses inside ourselves.

sections.md:
The essay ends with the writer saying that the climb changed him: he became more humble, more aware of nature's power and of his own smallness, and more determined to keep climbing the inner peaks.

**Tone:** reflective, sincere, spiritual, humble. **Style:** first person; short narrative moments mixed with reflections; rhetorical questions; images of height and depth.

**Themes:** courage and endurance; humility before nature; unity of faiths; the inner struggle; growth through challenge.

**Vocabulary** (meanings in our words): *exhilarating* — thrillingly happy; *ecstasy* — overwhelming joy; *humble* — modest; *awe* — wonder mixed with respect; *ascent / descent* — going up / coming down; *summit* — top.

**Grammar focus:** the exercises practise forming words and opposites (e.g. *ascent/descent*, *possible/impossible*), and ask you to write about a challenge you faced.

**Model answer — What qualities does a mountaineer need?** A mountaineer needs fitness and endurance to bear cold, thin air and exhaustion; persistence and will-power to go on after setbacks; teamwork and trust; and humility, because the mountain is never truly 'conquered'. The same qualities help us climb the inner summit.

**Did you know?** At 8,848 m the air holds only about one-third of the oxygen available at sea level, so most climbers use bottled oxygen.

summary: Writer: Major H.P.S. Ahluwalia, member of the 1965 Indian Everest expedition.
He felt joy, humility and a little sadness on the summit.
People climb for challenge, beauty, endurance and achievement.
Climbing brings one closer to nature and to God.
Offerings: Durga (Rawat), Buddha relic (Phu Dorji), Guru Nanak (Ahluwalia).
Hillary had buried a cross in 1953.
The descent is dangerous; success needs continued care.
The 'summit within' means conquering inner weaknesses.
The inner climb needs endurance, persistence and will-power.
The experience made the writer humble and changed his outlook.

Why do people climb mountains, according to the writer?
What offerings were left on the summit and what does this show?
Why does the writer say the descent matters?
Explain the title 'The Summit Within'.

Describe a challenge in your life that was your 'summit within'.

rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn.title: This is Jody's Fawn — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch06-jodys-fawn.subtitle: A boy, a dying doe, and a baby deer alone in the Florida woods

sections.h: The hook: a life for a life
sections.md:
A rattlesnake bites a father in the woods. To save him, he shoots a **doe** (a female deer), cuts out her heart and liver and presses them on the bite to draw out the poison. He lives. But somewhere in the bushes, the doe's newborn **fawn** is now alone. A boy can't stop thinking about it.

This chapter is taken from the American novel ***The Yearling*** (1938) by **Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings** (1896–1953), which won the Pulitzer Prize. It is set in the scrub forest of **Florida** among poor farming families. The author died in 1953, but because we are not certain of the exact wording of the textbook extract, this companion gives a **complete scene-by-scene retelling in our own words** with the meaning of every part. Read the original in your Honeydew book (link below).

**Characters**

| Who | Role |
|---|---|
| Jody Baxter | 11–12-year-old boy, kind and imaginative |
| Penny Baxter | his father, bitten by a rattlesnake |
| Ma Baxter | his mother, practical and firm |
| Doc Wilson | the doctor who treated Penny |
| Mill-wheel | son of the Forrester family, a neighbour |

Penny Baxter is recovering in bed after the snakebite. Doc Wilson has done his work. Jody cannot rest: he keeps thinking of the doe whose organs saved his father, and of her fawn, now motherless and probably starving.

He goes to his father and asks, gently, whether he may go and find the fawn and bring it home. Penny agrees at once: it is not right, he says, to repay the doe by leaving her baby to die. He says they took the mother; they owe the fawn its life. Ma Baxter is less happy — they barely have enough milk and food themselves — but Penny's word wins. Doc Wilson also says the boy is right.

**Meaning:** gratitude and responsibility. Penny teaches Jody that we owe something to those who help us, even animals.

check.q: Why does Penny agree that Jody should bring the fawn home?
options: Because they owed the doe for saving his life
check.why: Penny felt it would be ungrateful to let the fawn starve after its mother's death saved him.

sections.md:
Jody needs help to find the place. **Mill-wheel**, a Forrester boy, is riding back home and takes Jody along on his horse. On the way Jody worries that Mill-wheel might laugh at him or that the fawn might already be dead — eaten by wildcats or other animals.

Mill-wheel is a bit doubtful; he warns that the fawn may have been taken by an animal, and that a fawn raised by people grows up tame and later causes trouble. But he takes Jody to the spot where Penny shot the doe and says he will leave Jody there because Jody wants to look alone.

**Meaning:** Jody's determination. He wants to do the job himself, quietly.
keyTerms: Doe — female deer
Fawn — a baby deer
Yearling — an animal about one year old

sections.md:
Jody finds the body of the doe where it fell, with buzzards circling. He searches the area, following small hoof prints, and at last discovers the **fawn** curled up in a hidden nest of grass. It lifts its head and looks at him with big, wet eyes.

Jody is overwhelmed with tenderness. He strokes it; it doesn't run away. He feels its soft, spotted coat. He picks it up — its legs dangle — and carries it, staggering under its weight, through the woods. When he sets it down to rest, it follows him on wobbly legs, as if it knows him already.

**Meaning:** a deep bond forms instantly. The scene is full of sensory detail: smell of the woods, softness of the fawn, Jody's beating heart.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#e8f5e9'/><g fill='#2e7d32'><circle cx='70' cy='90' r='50'/><circle cx='530' cy='80' r='55'/><rect x='60' y='120' width='18' height='150' fill='#6d4c41'/><rect x='520' y='120' width='18' height='150' fill='#6d4c41'/></g><rect y='260' width='600' height='40' fill='#a5d6a7'/><g><ellipse cx='0' cy='238' rx='30' ry='16' fill='#c8915a'/><circle cx='28' cy='222' r='10' fill='#c8915a'/><g fill='#fff'><circle cx='-8' cy='232' r='2'/><circle cx='6' cy='236' r='2'/></g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' from='120 0' to='430 0' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g><rect x='-6' y='190' width='14' height='45' fill='#1565c0'/><circle cx='1' cy='180' r='12' fill='#f1c27d'/><rect x='-4' y='235' width='5' height='25' fill='#333'/><rect x='4' y='235' width='5' height='25' fill='#333'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' from='190 0' to='500 0' dur='7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><text x='300' y='30' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' text-anchor='middle'>The fawn follows Jody home</text></svg>
fig.caption: After a rest, the fawn trots behind Jody as if he were its mother.
fig.alt: Animated boy walking with a fawn following

sections.h: Scene 4: Home and a bottle of milk
sections.md:
Jody reaches home. Ma Baxter is not pleased, but she has agreed. The fawn will not drink milk from a bowl. Jody dips his fingers in the milk and lets it suck them; slowly it learns to drink from the gourd. Every time he moves, it follows him.

Penny watches with a smile. Jody feels that the fawn is truly his — the first thing that has ever belonged to him alone. He thinks of naming it (in the novel it becomes **Flag**, after its white tail).

**Meaning:** patience and care. Jody becomes a 'parent' and learns responsibility.

check.q: How did Jody get the fawn to drink milk?
options: He let it suck milk from his fingers
check.why: The fawn would not drink from a bowl, so Jody dipped his fingers in milk and let it suck them.

sections.md:
**Themes**
- *Compassion for animals* — Jody cannot bear the fawn to suffer.
- *Gratitude and debt* — the doe gave her life; the family repays by saving her baby.
- *Growing up* — Jody takes on adult responsibility.
- *Bond between humans and nature* — life in the scrub is hard, yet full of tenderness.

**Jody:** sensitive, kind, imaginative, determined, responsible. **Penny:** fair, wise, grateful; a gentle father. **Ma Baxter:** practical and worried about food, but not cruel. **Mill-wheel:** sceptical but helpful. **Doc Wilson:** supports Jody's idea.

**Style:** third-person narration close to Jody's feelings; American rural dialogue; rich nature imagery.

**Did you know?** In the full novel, the fawn grows into a yearling that eats the family's crops, leading to a heartbreaking ending — Jody's painful step into adulthood.

The exercises focus on:

- **Comprehension** of why Jody went, what Mill-wheel thought, and how the fawn responded.
- **Vocabulary of movement and sounds** — *stagger, wobble, bleat, trot*.
- **Adverbs** describing how things are done (*gently, slowly, firmly*).
- **Writing:** a paragraph on caring for a pet, or a debate on keeping wild animals at home.

**Model answer — Why did Jody want to bring the fawn home?** Jody knew his father's life had been saved by the doe's heart and liver. The doe's baby was now alone and would starve or be killed. Feeling grateful and sorry for it, he wanted to repay the mother by caring for the fawn.

**Model answer — How did the fawn respond to Jody?** At first it simply looked at him without fear. When he carried and then put it down, it followed him, and later it learnt to drink milk from his fingers. It treated him like a mother.

summary: Extract from 'The Yearling' (1938) by Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings, set in Florida.
Penny Baxter was bitten by a rattlesnake; he killed a doe to use her organs on the bite.
Jody worried about the doe's motherless fawn.
Penny agreed they owed the fawn its life; Ma Baxter reluctantly agreed.
Mill-wheel took Jody on horseback to the place.
Jody found the fawn in a nest of grass and carried it home.
The fawn followed him and learnt to suck milk from his fingers.
Themes: compassion, gratitude, responsibility, growing up.
Jody felt the fawn was truly his own.
practice: Why did Penny Baxter shoot the doe?
What made Jody think of the fawn?
What were Mill-wheel's doubts?
Describe how Jody found the fawn.
How did Jody feed the fawn?
What qualities of Jody does the story show?
Is it right to keep a wild animal as a pet? Give your view.
Write the story from the fawn's point of view.

rd-school-c8-english.ch07-visit-to-cambr.title: A Visit to Cambridge — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch07-visit-to-cambr.subtitle: A young writer in a wheelchair meets the greatest physicist of his time

sections.h: The hook: two men, two wheelchairs
sections.md:
What would you ask a genius who cannot move, cannot speak except through a computer, and yet explains the birth of the universe? **Firdaus Kanga**, a writer from Mumbai born with a condition that left his bones brittle and kept him in a wheelchair, had exactly that chance. While touring England, he visited **Cambridge** and met **Stephen Hawking** (1942–2018), the physicist with motor neurone disease (ALS) who wrote *A Brief History of Time*.

The chapter is taken from Kanga's travel book *Heaven on Wheels*. Because it is under copyright, this companion retells every part in our own words and explains its meaning. Read the original in your Honeydew book (link below).

**Did you know?** Hawking held the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge — the same post once held by Isaac Newton.

Kanga is on a trip through England, where he finds people more considerate of disability than he expected. In Cambridge he learns that Hawking lives there, and he desperately wants to meet him. He phones; to his surprise, he is told he may come and meet Hawking for a short while.

He goes with nervous excitement. He wonders whether it is right to take an ill man's precious time, and what he could possibly say that would be worth Hawking's effort to answer.

**Meaning:** Kanga admires Hawking not only for his science but because Hawking proves that disability need not stop a brilliant life — something Kanga longs to believe about himself.

check.q: From which book is 'A Visit to Cambridge' taken?
check.why: It is an extract from Firdaus Kanga's travelogue 'Heaven on Wheels'.

sections.md:
Kanga is taken into a room. Hawking sits in his motorised wheelchair, his head slightly to one side, body still. He communicates by pressing a switch to select words on a computer screen, which a **voice synthesiser** then speaks aloud in a flat, mechanical voice. Every sentence takes time.

Kanga feels awkward at first: he is aware that each of his questions costs Hawking minutes of effort. He describes the silence while Hawking composes answers, and the sound of the clicking switch.

He tells Hawking that he, too, is in a wheelchair, and talks of what it is like to be seen by others as 'brave'. Kanga notes, honestly, that people call disabled people brave when actually they often have no choice — they simply get on with life.

**Meaning:** a frank look at how society treats disabled people — with pity or false praise rather than respect.
keyTerms: Voice synthesiser — a machine that turns typed text into speech
Motor neurone disease — an illness that slowly stops nerves controlling muscles
Brittle — easily broken

sections.md:
Kanga asks Hawking what he finds most exciting or helpful in his life with disability. Hawking's answer (in our words): he **didn't think about the disability**; he kept his mind on his work, and he found it possible to do a great deal even with his body's limits. Kanga also asks if Hawking feels 'brave', and gets a quietly humorous, matter-of-fact reply.

Kanga then asks what advice he would give to disabled people. Hawking's message, as Kanga reports it: concentrate on what you **can** do well, and don't regret what you can't do. (This is an often-quoted idea of Hawking's; exact words are in the textbook.)

Kanga is moved almost to tears. Hawking smiles — a smile that Kanga says lights up his face — and Kanga feels the smile is worth everything.

**Meaning:** focus on abilities, not disabilities. The genius of Hawking's mind is not trapped by his body.

check.q: What was Hawking's advice to disabled people, as Kanga reports it?
options: Concentrate on what they can do well and not regret what they can't
check.why: Hawking urged focusing on one's abilities instead of regretting limitations.

sections.md:
As he leaves, Kanga wants to touch Hawking's hand, but hesitates, then does so gently. He feels something like a connection between two people who know what it is to live in a body that does not obey.

Outside, Kanga reflects that Hawking's life shows the 'bravest thing' is not some heroic act but simply living fully — thinking, laughing, working — inside limits. He also notes Hawking's humour: the great man's eyes still twinkle.

He goes on with his journey feeling inspired and more confident about his own life as a writer.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f3e5f5'/><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='60' fill='none' stroke='#7b1fa2' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='8' fill='#ffca28'><animate attributeName='r' values='6;14;6' dur='2s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></circle><g fill='#4a148c'><circle r='5'><animateMotion dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite' path='M240 150 A60 60 0 1 1 360 150 A60 60 0 1 1 240 150'/></circle></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle'><text x='300' y='40'>The mind roams the universe…</text><text x='300' y='270'>…while the body stays still</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Hawking's mind explored black holes and the Big Bang though his body could barely move.
fig.alt: Animated orbit around a glowing centre

sections.md:
**Themes**
- *Ability over disability*: what matters is what you can do.
- *Courage of everyday life*: true bravery is going on living fully.
- *Respect, not pity*: disabled people want equality, not sympathy.
- *Inspiration*: one life can light up another.

**Firdaus Kanga:** honest, witty, sensitive, self-aware; admires Hawking deeply. **Stephen Hawking:** brilliant, patient, humorous, positive.

**Tone:** personal, warm, sometimes funny, deeply moving. **Form:** travelogue / personal account in first person.

**Language work:** the exercises use the word *disabled* and related expressions, ask you to discuss how public spaces can be made accessible (ramps, lifts, Braille signs), and to look up books by Hawking. You may be asked to write about a person who overcame a challenge.

**Q. Why was Kanga nervous about meeting Hawking?** He knew Hawking could speak only slowly through a computer and that each answer cost him effort, so Kanga worried about wasting the great man's time with questions that were not worth it.

**Q. What does Kanga mean by 'brave'?** He means that people often call disabled people brave, though they simply live as well as they can because they have no other choice; real bravery is facing life every day.

**Q. What did Kanga learn from the visit?** He learnt that a person can lead a full, creative life despite severe disability by concentrating on his abilities.

**Did you know?** In India, the *Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016* requires public buildings and transport to be accessible to everyone.

summary: Writer: Firdaus Kanga; extract from 'Heaven on Wheels'.
Kanga uses a wheelchair because of brittle bones.
On a trip to England, he visited Cambridge to meet Stephen Hawking.
Hawking had motor neurone disease and spoke through a voice synthesiser.
Kanga felt guilty about taking Hawking's time.
They discussed being called 'brave'.
Hawking advised focusing on what one can do, without regret for what one can't.
Hawking's smile and humour moved Kanga.
Themes: ability over disability, everyday courage, respect not pity.
practice: Why did Kanga want to meet Stephen Hawking?
How did Hawking communicate?
Why did Kanga feel guilty during the meeting?
What did Kanga say about being called 'brave'?
What advice did Hawking give?

rd-school-c8-english.ch08-short-monsoon-.title: A Short Monsoon Diary — Chapter Companion
rd-school-c8-english.ch08-short-monsoon-.subtitle: Mist, leeches, a scarlet minivet and a mountain cottage — the monsoon through Ruskin Bond's window

sections.h: The hook: what does rain sound like on a tin roof?
sections.md:
Close your eyes. Rain drums on a tin roof. Mist creeps in through the window. A leopard coughs somewhere on the hillside, and a tiny bird flashes red in a dripping oak. This is the world of **Ruskin Bond** (born 1934), who has lived for decades in **Landour, near Mussoorie**, in the Garhwal Himalaya.

The chapter is a set of **diary entries** from one monsoon season, from June to March. Because Bond is a living author, this companion does not reproduce his words. It walks through **every entry in order**, retelling what he notices and explaining its meaning. Read the original in your Honeydew textbook (link below).

**Why a diary?** A diary is personal, dated, and written in the moment. It lets a writer record small, beautiful details that would be lost in a formal essay. Bond's diary shows how to *observe*.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><linearGradient id='k' x1='0' y1='0' x2='0' y2='1'><stop offset='0' stop-color='#607d8b'/><stop offset='1' stop-color='#cfd8dc'/></linearGradient><style>.d{stroke:#90caf9;stroke-width:2;animation:f 1s linear infinite}@keyframes f{from{transform:translateY(-40px)}to{transform:translateY(300px)}}</style></defs><rect width='600' height='300' fill='url(#k)'/><polygon points='0,300 150,160 300,300' fill='#455a64'/><polygon points='200,300 380,130 560,300' fill='#37474f'/><rect x='360' y='220' width='80' height='50' fill='#8d6e63'/><polygon points='350,220 400,190 450,220' fill='#b0bec5'/><g><line class='d' x1='50' y1='0' x2='45' y2='20'/><line class='d' x1='140' y1='0' x2='135' y2='20' style='animation-delay:.3s'/><line class='d' x1='240' y1='0' x2='235' y2='20' style='animation-delay:.6s'/><line class='d' x1='330' y1='0' x2='325' y2='20' style='animation-delay:.2s'/><line class='d' x1='430' y1='0' x2='425' y2='20' style='animation-delay:.5s'/><line class='d' x1='530' y1='0' x2='525' y2='20' style='animation-delay:.8s'/></g><ellipse cx='300' cy='200' rx='260' ry='22' fill='#fff' opacity='.35'><animate attributeName='cx' values='260;340;260' dur='8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse></svg>
fig.caption: Rain over a hill cottage; mist drifting through the valley.
fig.alt: Animated rain over hills and a cottage

sections.h: June 24 & 25: Mist and the first rain
sections.md:
**June 24:** Mist fills the valley; it rises through the trees and enters the room like a ghost. Bond watches it hide the hills completely, then thin away. Nature plays hide-and-seek.

**June 25:** The first heavy rain falls, and the first sign is the smell — the rich scent of wet earth. Rain on the tin roof drums hard; birds go quiet; frogs begin. He loves the sound because it makes the house feel cosy.

**Meaning:** the monsoon arrives with mist and smell before sight. Bond notices with all five senses.

check.q: What does Bond notice first about the arriving rain?
check.why: The fragrant smell of rain on dry earth announces the monsoon.

sections.md:
**June 26:** Birds in the forest are busy even in the rain. Bond spots a **scarlet minivet**, a small bird with flame-red plumage, darting among wet trees, and a **whistling thrush** singing.

**June 27:** A leopard is said to be in the area. Bond hears from villagers that the leopard had taken a dog. Even so, he goes walking; he feels the leopard, though dangerous, belongs to the forest just as the people do.

**Meaning:** human and wild life share the hillside. Bond respects wildlife without fear-mongering.
keyTerms: Scarlet minivet — a small Himalayan bird; male is bright red
Whistling thrush — a bird with a beautiful whistling song
Fern — a non-flowering green plant of damp places

sections.md:
In **July**, the rain hardly stops.

- **Leeches** appear everywhere on the paths; they slip into shoes and suck blood. Bond is matter-of-fact: they are a nuisance but part of the season.
- **Plants** burst out: ferns, wild flowers, creepers climb walls and fill gaps. Even the cracks in the stone wall turn green.
- The **cicadas** fall silent in heavy rain, then start again.

**Meaning:** the monsoon is not only pretty; it is a season of extreme growth, damp and small pests. Bond writes honestly about both sides.

**August** brings rain day after day. Bond describes the forest becoming wild and lush, and a cobra lily (a plant that looks like a snake's hood) rising from the forest floor. A huge trunk of moss-covered oak glistens.

He also notices how the animals behave: birds huddle; insects swarm toward his lamp at night. A **brain-fever bird** (common hawk-cuckoo) calls repeatedly. He mentions how difficult it is to dry clothes — everything is damp.

**Meaning:** observation of the cycle of life; rain as both trouble and gift.

check.q: What is the cobra lily?
options: A plant shaped like a cobra's hood
check.why: It is a monsoon plant whose shape resembles a snake's hood.

sections.h: September: Rain ends, and moths arrive
sections.md:
In **September** the rains slowly withdraw. On some days the sun comes out and the hills shine clean. Bond describes the beauty of a clear sky after weeks of cloud, and of the first glimpse of the far snow peaks.

At night, **moths** of all sizes and colours gather at his window lamp — some as big as birds. He enjoys them as part of the season's show. He notes the 'cicada orchestra' too.

**Meaning:** every season has its end; the writer welcomes the change calmly.

sections.h: Winter to March: The year turns
sections.md:
The diary jumps ahead. In winter, rain is cold and grey; snow sometimes falls. In **March**, Bond notes a heavy shower or hailstorm and the first warm sun; birds return; spring flowers appear. He reflects that the seasons come round like an old friend.

A lovely closing idea: the world outside his window — rain, birds, mist, children going to school with umbrellas — is a story in itself, if only one looks.

**Did you know?** Landour is at about 2,200 m; monsoon clouds from the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea reach it in late June.

**Themes:** love of nature; joy in small things; the harmony of humans and wildlife; the rhythm of seasons.

**Style:** dated diary entries; first person; simple, vivid images; sensory words (sound of rain, smell of earth, sight of mist, feel of damp); gentle humour.

**Language work in the exercises:** using *simple present* for diary observations, collecting words for weather (*drizzle, downpour, mist, fog, hail*), and writing your own diary entry about a rainy day.

**Model answer — How does Bond show his love of nature?** He notices tiny details others would miss — the colour of a minivet, the smell of the first rain, the shapes of moths, the mist entering his room. He accepts even leeches and leopards as part of the hills. His calm, affectionate tone shows that nature is his companion.

summary: Writer: Ruskin Bond, living in Landour near Mussoorie.
The chapter is a set of diary entries across the monsoon and beyond.
Mist enters the room like a ghost; the first rain smells of wet earth.
Birds: scarlet minivet, whistling thrush, brain-fever bird.
A leopard lives near the village; Bond respects it.
July brings leeches, ferns and creepers.
August brings constant rain and the cobra lily.
September brings clear skies and moths.
Winter and March complete the cycle of seasons.
Style: sensory, simple, affectionate, dated entries.
practice: What does Bond see when mist fills the valley?
How does the first rain announce itself?
Name the birds Bond mentions and describe one.
What are Bond's feelings about leeches and the leopard?
What is a cobra lily?
How do things change in September?
Write a diary entry about a rainy day in your town.
Why is a diary a good form for writing about nature?

rd-school-c8-english.grammar-class8.title: English Grammar for Class 8 — The Complete Companion
rd-school-c8-english.grammar-class8.subtitle: Tenses, voice, reported speech, modals, clauses and more — explained with Indian examples

sections.md:
Grammar is like the rules of cricket. You can hit the ball without knowing them, but you can't play a match. Every Honeydew chapter has a grammar exercise; this read gathers them all in one place: **parts of speech, tenses, subject–verb agreement, active/passive voice, reported speech, modals, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, clauses, phrasal verbs, determiners, and punctuation**.

**The eight parts of speech**

| Part | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | names | Priya, Delhi, courage |
| Pronoun | replaces a noun | she, it, they |
| Verb | action/state | run, is, seems |
| Adjective | describes noun | tall, red, five |
| Adverb | describes verb/adj | quickly, very |
| Preposition | relation | in, on, under |
| Conjunction | joins | and, but, because |
| Interjection | emotion | Wow! Oh! |

check.q: In 'She ran very fast', what is 'very'?
check.why: 'Very' modifies the adverb 'fast', so it is an adverb.

sections.md:
English has three times (present, past, future) and four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).

| | Simple | Continuous | Perfect | Perfect continuous |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Present | I play | I am playing | I have played | I have been playing |
| Past | I played | I was playing | I had played | I had been playing |
| Future | I will play | I will be playing | I will have played | I will have been playing |

**Key uses**
- Simple present: habits, facts (*The sun rises in the east.*)
- Present perfect: past action with present result (*I have lost my key.*)
- Past perfect: the earlier of two past actions (*The train had left when we reached.*)
- *since* for a point of time, *for* for a period (*since 2020, for three years*).

sections.md:
A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb.

- *The boy **plays**. The boys **play**.*
- *Each of the students **has** a book.* (each = singular)
- *Neither Ravi nor his friends **are** late.* (verb agrees with nearer subject)
- *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast.* (one idea)
- *The team **is** winning.* (as a unit)
- *Mathematics **is** easy; the news **is** good.*

check.q: Choose the correct verb: 'One of my friends ___ from Pune.'
check.why: The subject is 'one', which is singular, so 'is'.

sections.md:
In the **active** voice the doer comes first; in the **passive** the receiver comes first, and the verb becomes *be + past participle*.

| Tense | Active | Passive |
|---|---|---|
| Simple present | Ravi writes a letter. | A letter is written by Ravi. |
| Present continuous | Ravi is writing a letter. | A letter is being written by Ravi. |
| Simple past | Ravi wrote a letter. | A letter was written by Ravi. |
| Present perfect | Ravi has written a letter. | A letter has been written by Ravi. |
| Future | Ravi will write a letter. | A letter will be written by Ravi. |
| Modal | Ravi can write it. | It can be written by Ravi. |

Use passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant: *The bridge was built in 1880.*

**Rules when the reporting verb is in the past:**

1. Remove quotation marks; add *that* (statements), *if/whether* (yes–no questions) or the wh-word.
2. Shift tense back: *is → was, are → were, has → had, will → would, can → could, went → had gone*.
3. Change pronouns and time words: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that*.
4. Commands: *told/ordered/requested + to + verb*.

Universal truths keep their tense: *The teacher said that the earth goes round the sun.*

Modals help the main verb show ability, permission, possibility, obligation.

| Modal | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| can / could | ability, permission | I can swim. Could I come in? |
| may / might | permission, possibility | It may rain. |
| must | strong duty, certainty | You must wear a helmet. |
| should / ought to | advice | You should sleep early. |
| will / would | future, polite request | Would you help me? |
| need not | no necessity | You need not hurry. |
| must have / might have | guess about past | He must have missed the bus. |

check.q: Which modal shows strong obligation?
check.why: 'Must' expresses a strong duty or necessity.

sections.md:
**Adverbs** tell *how, when, where, how often, how much*: *slowly, yesterday, here, always, very*. Many adjectives form adverbs with *-ly* (*careful → carefully*); some are irregular (*good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard*).

**Prepositions of time:** *at* 5 o'clock, *on* Monday/15 August, *in* July/2025/the morning. **Of place:** *at* the station, *on* the table, *in* the room. Others: *between* two, *among* many; *beside* (next to), *besides* (in addition).

**Conjunctions:** coordinating (*and, but, or, so, yet*) join equal parts; subordinating (*because, although, when, if, unless, since, while*) begin a dependent clause. Correlatives: *either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and*.

**Clauses:** a *main clause* stands alone; a *subordinate clause* cannot.
- Noun clause: *I know **that he is honest**.*
- Adjective (relative) clause: *The girl **who won** is my sister.* (who/which/that/whose/whom)
- Adverb clause: *We stayed in **because it rained**.*

**Sentence types:** simple (one clause), compound (two main clauses joined by *and/but*), complex (main + subordinate).

**Phrasal verbs** (Honeydew exercises love these): *look after* (care for), *look up* (search), *give up* (stop), *put off* (postpone), *run out of* (have none left), *break down* (stop working), *take after* (resemble), *come across* (find by chance).

**Determiners:** *a/an/the, this/that, some/any, much/many, few/a few, little/a little*. *A few* = some; *few* = hardly any.

check.q: 'Please ___ the meeting till Friday' means postpone. Which phrasal verb fits?
check.why: 'Put off' means to postpone.

sections.md:
- **Full stop** ends statements; **question mark** ends questions; **exclamation mark** for strong feeling.
- **Comma** separates items in a list, after introductory words, around extra information.
- **Apostrophe**: possession (*Ravi's bat, the girls' room*) and contraction (*it's = it is*; *its* = belonging to it).
- **Inverted commas** for direct speech: *Mother said, "Come home."*
- **Capital letters**: start of sentence, proper nouns, *I*.

**Common Indian-English slips:** *I am having a car* → *I have a car*; *discuss about* → *discuss*; *return back* → *return*; *cousin brother* → *cousin*; *one of my friend* → *one of my friends*.

workedExamples.q: Change to passive: The children are planting trees.
steps: Present continuous passive: are being + past participle.
workedExamples.answer: Trees are being planted by the children.

workedExamples.q: Report: Meena said, "I will go to Shimla tomorrow."
steps: will → would; tomorrow → the next day.
workedExamples.answer: Meena said that she would go to Shimla the next day.

workedExamples.q: Report: The teacher said to Arjun, "Close the door."
workedExamples.answer: The teacher told Arjun to close the door.

workedExamples.q: Report: He asked me, "Are you hungry?"
workedExamples.answer: He asked me if I was hungry.

workedExamples.q: Combine using a relative clause: I met a man. He had climbed Everest.
workedExamples.answer: I met a man who had climbed Everest.

workedExamples.q: Correct: She don't like tea since three years.
steps: Period of time → 'for'; present perfect for continuing state.
workedExamples.answer: She hasn't liked tea for three years. / She doesn't like tea.

summary: Eight parts of speech each do a job.
Twelve tense forms: 3 times × 4 aspects.
Since + point of time; for + period.
Verb agrees with subject; 'each/one of' are singular.
Passive = be + past participle; object becomes subject.
Reported speech shifts tense, pronouns and time words.
Modals show ability, permission, possibility, obligation.
Adverbs answer how/when/where; prepositions show relation.
Clauses: noun, adjective (relative), adverb.
Phrasal verbs change meaning with particles.
Apostrophe: it's = it is; its = possessive.
practice: Change into passive: The police arrested the thief.
Report: Rahul said, "I am reading a novel now."
Fill in: She has lived here ___ 2018.
Choose: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ (was/were) present.
Use 'must have' in a sentence about something that happened yesterday.
Combine with 'although': It was raining. We played cricket.
Write five sentences using phrasal verbs with 'look'.
Correct the errors: Each of the boys have their own bicycle.
Punctuate: ravi said where is my bat
Identify the clause: The book that you gave me is exciting.

rd-school-c8-english.revision-practice.title: Class 8 English — The Whole-Book Revision
rd-school-c8-english.revision-practice.subtitle: Every Honeydew chapter and poem, plus It So Happened, in one guided revision

sections.h: How to revise a whole book in a week
sections.md:
Exams are close and the book feels huge. Here is a plan:

| Day | Task |
|---|---|
| 1 | Prose chapters 1–3 + poems 1–3 |
| 2 | Prose 4–6 + poems 4–5 |
| 3 | Prose 7–10 + poems 6–8 |
| 4 | Supplementary reader *It So Happened* |
| 5 | Grammar: tenses, voice, reported speech, modals |
| 6 | Writing: letter, notice, diary, paragraph |
| 7 | Full mock paper, timed |

For each chapter know: **author, genre, characters, plot in 5 points, theme, one moral, and two likely questions**. The sections below give exactly that, in our own words. Read the full texts in your textbook (links at the end).

check.q: What should you know for every chapter?
options: Author, characters, plot, theme and likely questions
check.why: Knowing author, characters, plot, theme and likely questions prepares you for any type of question.

sections.md:
**1. The Best Christmas Present in the World** (Michael Morpurgo). The narrator buys an old desk and finds a secret drawer with a 1914 letter from soldier **Jim Macpherson** to his wife **Connie**, describing the Christmas truce when British and German soldiers played football in no-man's-land. The narrator finds Connie, now very old in a nursing home; she thinks he is Jim come back. *Theme:* peace, love, futility of war.

**2. The Tsunami** (2004 Indian Ocean tsunami). True stories: **Ignesious** (Andaman) loses family members; **Meghna** survives two days at sea; **Almas** loses her family; **Tilly Smith**, a 10-year-old British girl in Phuket, recognises the signs from a geography lesson and saves a beach; animals sense danger and flee to high ground. *Theme:* awareness saves lives; nature's power.

check.q: Who saved people on a Phuket beach by recognising tsunami signs?
check.why: Tilly Smith remembered her geography lesson and warned others.

sections.md:
**3. Glimpses of the Past** — picture-story of 1757–1857: divided rulers, Company power, ruined farmers and weavers, Ram Mohan Roy's reforms, sepoys' grievances, revolt of 1857. *Theme:* disunity and exploitation lead to rebellion.

**4. Bepin Choudhury's Lapse of Memory** (Satyajit Ray) — a stranger, Parimal Ghosh, insists Bepin visited Ranchi in 1958; friend Dinesh confirms; Bepin fears madness, sees a doctor, visits Ranchi, collapses; a letter from **Chunilal** reveals the trick, played because Bepin had refused to help him. *Theme:* pride, friendship.

**5. The Summit Within** (Maj. H.P.S. Ahluwalia) — feelings on Everest's summit: joy, humility, sadness; offerings of faiths; the inner climb against our weaknesses. *Theme:* self-conquest.

**6. This is Jody's Fawn** (Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings) — Penny is bitten by a rattlesnake and kills a doe to use her organs; Jody rescues her fawn with Mill-wheel's help and feeds it milk from his fingers. *Theme:* compassion, gratitude.

**7. A Visit to Cambridge** (Firdaus Kanga) — the wheelchair-using writer meets Stephen Hawking; talks about being called 'brave'; Hawking advises focusing on what you can do. *Theme:* ability over disability.

**8. A Short Monsoon Diary** (Ruskin Bond) — dated entries from Landour: mist, first rain, minivet, leopard, leeches, cobra lily, moths, end of the rains. *Theme:* love of nature, observation.

**9–10. The Great Stone Face I & II** (Nathaniel Hawthorne, d.1864) — in a valley, a rock on the mountain looks like a noble human face; a prophecy says a great man resembling it will come. Young **Ernest** waits all his life. Rich **Mr. Gathergold**, the general **Old Blood-and-Thunder**, the politician **Old Stony Phiz** and finally a **poet** each seem to fulfil it, but none does. At last the poet sees that Ernest himself — humble, wise, good — resembles the Great Stone Face. Ernest modestly hopes a wiser man will come. *Theme:* true greatness is goodness and humility, not wealth, power or fame.

check.q: In 'The Great Stone Face', who finally resembles the face?
check.why: The poet recognises that Ernest, through his goodness and wisdom, resembles the Great Stone Face.

sections.md:
| Poem | Poet | Gist |
|---|---|---|
| The Ant and the Cricket | adapted from Aesop | carefree cricket starves in winter; ant refuses to lend: plan ahead |
| Geography Lesson | Zulfikar Ghose | from a plane, the logic of cities and rivers is clear, yet people still fight |
| Macavity: The Mystery Cat | T.S. Eliot | a master-criminal cat who is never there when the crime is found |
| The Last Bargain | Rabindranath Tagore | a king, an old man's gold and a girl's smile can't hire the speaker; a child playing 'for nothing' frees him |
| The School Boy | William Blake | a child loves summer mornings, hates the cage of school |
| The Duck and the Kangaroo | Edward Lear | duck rides on kangaroo's back with socks and a cloak — friendship and compromise |
| When I set out for Lyonnesse | Thomas Hardy | a journey that changed the poet; magic in his eyes on return |
| On the Grasshopper and Cricket | John Keats | 'the poetry of earth is never dead' — the grasshopper in summer, cricket in winter |

**Poetic devices to spot:** rhyme scheme, alliteration, personification (Keats), repetition (Macavity), metaphor (the school as a cage), irony (Geography Lesson).

check.q: Which poem says that the poetry of earth never ceases?
check.why: Keats's sonnet celebrates the grasshopper and cricket keeping nature's song alive in every season.

sections.md:
1. **How the Camel Got His Hump** (Kipling) — a lazy camel says 'Humph'; the Djinn gives him a hump to work three days without food.
2. **Children at Work** — Velu runs away to Chennai and ends up picking rags; theme: child labour.
3. **The Selfish Giant** (Oscar Wilde) — walls out children, gets endless winter; opens garden, finds love.
4. **The Treasure Within** — Hafeez Contractor, architect, poor at school but creative.
5. **Princess September** (Somerset Maugham) — a caged bird stops singing; freedom matters.
6. **The Fight** — Ranji and Suraj fight over a pool, become friends.
7. **The Open Window** (Saki) — Vera's tall tale scares nervous Framton Nuttel.
8. **Jalebis** — a boy spends school-fee money on jalebis, guilt follows.
9. **The Comet I & II** — Duggal discovers a comet heading towards Earth.
10. **Ancient Education System of India** — gurukuls, Takshashila, Nalanda.

**Reference-to-context questions:** identify speaker, listener, situation, and meaning of the line.

**Long answers (100–150 words):** open with a one-line direct answer; give three supporting points from the text; end with a line on theme or your view.

**Value-based questions:** connect the text to life — e.g. Tilly Smith shows why paying attention in class matters; Ernest shows greatness lies in character.

**Time plan for 80 marks / 3 hours:** reading 20 min, writing 40 min, grammar 30 min, literature 75 min, checking 15 min.

**Did you know?** Examiners reward answers that use the character's name and a short detail from the text — it proves you've read the chapter.

summary: Honeydew has ten prose units and eight poems.
Christmas truce letter — peace and love.
Tsunami — Tilly Smith and survivors; awareness saves lives.
Glimpses of the Past — 1757–1857 picture-story.
Bepin — Chunilal's trick teaches a lesson about friendship.
Summit Within — inner climb.
Jody's Fawn — gratitude and compassion.
Visit to Cambridge — ability over disability.
Monsoon Diary — observing nature.
Great Stone Face — Ernest's goodness is true greatness.
Poems: Keats, Blake, Tagore, Eliot, Lear, Hardy, Ghose, Aesop-based.
It So Happened has ten stories and essays.
Answer structure: direct answer, three points, theme.
practice: How did the Christmas truce of 1914 show the futility of war?
How did animals react to the tsunami?
Why did Chunilal play a trick on Bepin Choudhury?
What is the 'summit within'?
Why did Jody want to bring the fawn home?
What advice did Stephen Hawking give Firdaus Kanga?
Describe the four men who were thought to resemble the Great Stone Face.
Explain the central idea of 'The Last Bargain'.
Why does the school boy compare himself to a caged bird?
Write a diary entry as Tilly Smith on the day of the tsunami.

rd-school-c8-english.supplementary-it-so.title: It So Happened — Supplementary Reader Companion
rd-school-c8-english.supplementary-it-so.subtitle: Ten stories: a grumpy camel, a selfish giant, a runaway boy, a comet and a tall tale at an open window

sections.h: 1. How the Camel Got His Hump (Rudyard Kipling)
sections.md:
From Kipling's *Just So Stories* (1902). In the early days of the world, animals began working for Man. The **Horse**, the **Dog** and the **Ox** each came to the Camel, who lived in the middle of a howling desert, eating thorns and refusing to work. To every request he replied only **'Humph!'**.

The three complained to Man, who said they must work double to make up. Angry, they took their case to the **Djinn in charge of All Deserts**. The Djinn found the Camel admiring his reflection in a pool and asked him to work. 'Humph!' said the Camel. The Djinn warned him not to say it again; the Camel said it again — and his back swelled into a great lolloping **hump**. The Djinn explained that the hump lets him work **three days without eating**, making up for the three days he had idled. The Camel has carried it ever since and has never learnt to behave.

**Moral:** idleness brings its own punishment; everyone must share the work. **Style:** playful 'just so' explanation of nature, repeated refrains, humour.

check.q: Why did the Djinn give the Camel a hump?
options: To let him work three days without eating, making up for idleness
check.why: The hump let him work three days without food to make up for the three days he had shirked.

sections.h: 2. Children at Work (Gita Wolf & Ali Saberi, adapted)
sections.md:
Eleven-year-old **Velu** runs away from his village, where his father beats him and there is little to eat. After two days on a train without a ticket, he arrives at **Chennai Central**, frightened by the crowds. A girl, **Jaya**, in torn clothes, finds him, buys him food and takes him to the 'Akka' (elder sister) who employs children to **pick rags** from garbage heaps — plastic, paper, glass, which are sold for recycling. Jaya shows him the city at night and explains the work. Velu is disgusted but has no choice; he joins her.

**Theme:** child labour and street children. **Meaning:** the story asks us to see children who sort waste in Indian cities as real children with fears and hopes. **Did you know?** India's Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act bans children under 14 from all work, and the Right to Education Act guarantees free schooling to age 14.

Children love to play in a **Giant's** beautiful garden. Returning after seven years with his friend, the Cornish ogre, the Giant drives them out, builds a high wall and puts up a sign forbidding trespass. Spring comes everywhere else, but in his garden it stays **winter**: Snow, Frost, the North Wind and Hail live there happily.

One morning he hears a linnet sing. The children have crept in through a hole and spring has returned with them — except in one corner where a tiny boy cannot climb a tree. The Giant's heart melts; he lifts the boy into the tree, knocks down the wall, and the garden becomes the children's playground. The little boy, however, never comes back, and the Giant longs for him.

Years later, old and weak, the Giant sees the little boy under a tree covered in white blossom. The child's hands and feet bear **wounds of love**. He tells the Giant that since the Giant once let him play in his garden, today he will take the Giant to *his* garden, Paradise. The children find the Giant dead under the tree, covered with white blossoms.

**Theme:** selfishness brings coldness; love and sharing bring spring. The child represents Christ (a Christian allegory).

check.q: What happened when the Giant built a wall around his garden?
options: Winter stayed there while spring came elsewhere
check.why: Without children, spring refused to come and winter stayed in the garden.

sections.md:
This is an interview with **Hafeez Contractor**, one of India's best-known architects. As a schoolboy in Mumbai he was poor at studies, especially maths, and was often in trouble for mischief. But he loved drawing and was imaginative.

He got into architecture almost by chance: an uncle suggested it, and he later trained under an architect while studying, eventually topping his class. He talks about how his teacher tells him to make a 'stamp' of his own, how he designs buildings by imagining them as a whole, and how children's creativity should not be crushed.

**Meaning:** not every talent shows in marks; parents and teachers should let children discover the 'treasure within'.

The King of Siam has nine daughters named after months. On his birthday the eight elder princesses receive parrots in gold cages; when September's parrot dies, a little **bird** flies in and sings beautifully for her. She is happy, but her jealous sisters warn that it may fly away, so she shuts it in a cage. The bird stops singing and grows weak. September realises it cannot live without freedom, lets it go, and it returns to sing to her every day, free.

**Theme:** love means giving freedom; possessiveness kills joy. **Did you know?** Siam is the old name of Thailand.

**Ranji**, new to Dehra from Rajasthan, discovers a secret forest pool and swims there. **Suraj**, a local boy, claims the pool as his own. They argue over who owns it and fight — first wrestling, then in the water — and neither wins. The next day they meet again; Suraj shows Ranji how to dive, and they become friends.

**Theme:** pride turns to friendship when rivals respect each other's strength.

**Framton Nuttel**, a nervous man sent to the countryside for a 'nerve cure', visits Mrs Sappleton. Her 15-year-old niece **Vera** entertains him while he waits. She points to the open French window and tells him a tragic tale: three years ago her aunt's husband and two brothers went shooting through that window and were swallowed by a bog; their bodies were never found, and her aunt keeps the window open expecting them back.

Mrs Sappleton enters and chats cheerfully about her husband and brothers coming back from shooting. Framton is horrified. Then three figures appear on the lawn with guns and a spaniel. Framton grabs his hat and flees. When the aunt wonders why, Vera calmly invents another tale — that he is terrified of dogs because he was once chased by pariah dogs in India. The last line tells us that **romance at short notice was her speciality**.

**Theme:** the power of storytelling; a twist ending.

check.q: What was Vera's 'speciality'?
check.why: Saki ends by saying that romance (made-up stories) at short notice was Vera's speciality.

sections.md:
A schoolboy carries four rupees for his school fees. On the way, the smell of hot **jalebis** tempts him. At school, the fee is waived for him because of his scholarship, so the coins burn in his pocket. They seem to speak, urging him to spend them. He buys a huge pile of jalebis, gives them away to children and eats till he feels sick, then feels deeply guilty. He prays for a miracle to replace the money, and resolves to become a good boy.

**Theme:** temptation and conscience; humour mixed with guilt.

**Part I:** Amateur astronomer **Duggal**, a retired civil servant, discovers a new comet through his telescope. It is named after him. Scientists calculate that the comet is on a path that may **collide with Earth**. The world panics; India's top scientists meet; Duggal is asked to help.

**Part II:** A plan is made to deflect the comet using rockets, but it fails. Then calculations show the comet will pass very close but miss. The comet's tail brushes Earth's atmosphere, causing spectacular light; no harm results. Duggal reflects on human co-operation in the face of a shared danger.

**Theme:** science, co-operation and calm reason over fear. Narlikar is a renowned Indian astrophysicist.

This essay explains learning in ancient India. Education began at home and in **gurukuls**, where students lived with the teacher and learnt through listening, memorising and discussion; it was free, the student served the guru, and a gift (*guru dakshina*) was given at the end. Subjects included the Vedas, grammar, logic, medicine, astronomy, mathematics and arts.

Buddhist **viharas** and great universities like **Takshashila** and **Nalanda** attracted students from China, Korea and Tibet; the Chinese travellers **Faxian** and **Xuanzang** described Nalanda's libraries. Women scholars like **Gargi** and **Maitreyi** are mentioned. The essay ends by linking this tradition to India's modern goals of holistic education.

**Theme:** India's long heritage of learning.

sections.h: Why writing marks are the easiest to win
sections.md:
In most Class 8 papers, writing tasks carry 15–20 marks. Unlike literature, you don't need to remember anything — only a **format**, a **plan** and **clear sentences**. Examiners usually mark in three parts:

| Criterion | What they look for |
|---|---|
| Format | correct layout (address, date, subject, signature) |
| Content | all points asked, relevant ideas |
| Expression | grammar, spelling, linking words, word limit |

**The 3-minute plan:** read the question twice; underline *who* writes, *to whom*, *about what*, and the *word limit*; jot 4–5 points; then write.

sections.md:
Used for principals, editors, officials, companies.

**Format:**
1. Sender's address
2. Date
3. Receiver's designation and address
4. Subject (one line)
5. Salutation: *Sir/Madam* or *Respected Sir*
6. Body: para 1 — purpose; para 2 — details; para 3 — request/action
7. Closing: *Yours faithfully* (or *Yours sincerely* if you know the name)
8. Signature, name

**Model (letter to the editor):**

> 12, Gandhi Nagar, Jaipur
> 27 November 2026
> The Editor, *The Rajasthan Times*, Jaipur
> Subject: Stray cattle on city roads
> Sir, Through your newspaper I wish to draw attention to stray cattle on MI Road, which cause accidents every week… I request the Municipal Corporation to set up shelters… Yours faithfully, Aarav Sharma

Keep tone polite, facts specific, and sentences short.

check.q: Which closing suits a formal letter to 'Sir'?
check.why: 'Yours faithfully' is the standard closing for formal letters addressed as Sir/Madam.

sections.md:
To friends and family. **Format:** your address, date, *Dear Riya*, body (friendly, personal, can ask questions), *Yours lovingly / Your friend*, name. No subject line.

**Content tips:** begin by responding to the reader (*Thank you for your letter…*), share news in two or three paragraphs, end with good wishes.

**Emails:** To, Cc, Subject, greeting, short paragraphs, closing, name. Even formal emails are shorter than letters; never write a whole email in capitals.

**Notice** — public announcement, put in a box, about 50 words.

| NOTICE (box) |
|---|
| Name of school |
| NOTICE (centred) |
| Date |
| Heading (e.g. INTER-HOUSE QUIZ) |
| What, when, where, who can join, whom to contact |
| Signature, name, designation (e.g. Head Girl) |

**Message** — a short note for someone who missed a call/visit, about 50 words, in a box: *Date, time, Dear…, message (who called, what, action needed), name.* Convert direct speech into reported form: *Uncle called to say he will reach at 7 p.m.*

check.q: What must a notice always include?
options: Date, heading, details and the issuer's name and designation
check.why: A notice needs date, heading, key details and who issued it.

sections.md:
Personal, reflective, first person, usually past tense for events and present for feelings.

**Format:** date (and day, time optional), *Dear Diary* (optional), body, signature/name.

**Model idea:** *Friday, 27 November 2026, 9 p.m. — Today our team lost the final by two runs. I dropped an easy catch and felt terrible. But Coach patted my back and said that every great fielder has dropped catches… Tomorrow I will practise for an extra hour.*

Include **what happened, how you felt, what you learnt**. (Compare Ruskin Bond's *A Short Monsoon Diary* for observation.)

A good paragraph has a **topic sentence**, **3–4 supporting sentences** with examples, and a **concluding sentence**.

**Describing a person:** appearance → personality → an incident that shows it → your feeling.
**Describing a place:** location → sights, sounds, smells → people → why it matters.
**Describing an event:** when/where → sequence (first, then, after that, finally) → highlight → feelings.

**Use sensory words:** *the aroma of ginger tea, the clatter of a local train, the hush before the monsoon*. **Avoid** repeating *nice, good, very*.

Often you get a beginning or outline. Use the **story mountain**: introduction (who, where) → problem → rising action → climax → resolution → moral/ending line. Give it a title.

**Tips:** past tense throughout; a little dialogue; a surprise if possible; 150–200 words.

**Mini-model:** *The Last Train* — Kabir misses the 10 p.m. train at Nagpur; a stranger offers a lift; Kabir hesitates, recalls his mother's advice, calls home instead; his father arrives; next day the news reports a gang posing as helpers was caught. Ending: trust your instincts.

check.q: What comes just before the resolution in a story mountain?
check.why: The climax is the high point of tension, followed by the resolution.

sections.md:
**Speech:** greeting (*Respected Principal, teachers and my dear friends*), introduce yourself and topic, 3 points with examples, conclusion, *Thank you*.

**Debate:** same greeting; state *for* or *against* the motion clearly; give arguments; rebut the other side politely; strong final line.

**Article:** title, *By (name)*, introduction with a hook, 2–3 body paragraphs, conclusion with suggestions. Topics: plastic pollution, screen time, importance of libraries, water conservation.

**Linking words to score:** *firstly, moreover, however, on the other hand, as a result, in conclusion.*

- Missing date or subject in a letter.
- Mixing formal and informal tone.
- Exceeding or falling short of the word limit by a lot.
- Spelling: *receive, believe, necessary, separate, accommodation*.
- Run-on sentences: use full stops.
- Forgetting a title for stories and articles.

**Did you know?** Reading one newspaper editorial a day for a month noticeably improves your vocabulary and sentence variety.

summary: Writing is marked on format, content and expression.
Plan before writing: who, to whom, what, word limit.
Formal letter: addresses, date, subject, Sir/Madam, Yours faithfully.
Informal letter: friendly, no subject line.
Notice: boxed, dated, headed, signed with designation.
Message: short, boxed, reported speech.
Diary: date, feelings, reflection, first person.
Paragraph: topic sentence, support, conclusion.
Story: story mountain and a title.
Speech/debate/article: greeting or title, 3 points, conclusion.

rd-school-c8-hindi.lekhan-pathan.title: रचनात्मक लेखन और अपठित (कक्षा 8) — संपूर्ण साथी
rd-school-c8-hindi.lekhan-pathan.subtitle: पत्र, निबंध, सूचना, संवाद, विज्ञापन, कहानी और अपठित गद्यांश–पद्यांश — आदर्श उत्तरों के साथ

sections.h: लेखन में अंक कैसे मिलते हैं?
sections.md:
परीक्षा में लेखन के प्रश्न सबसे भरोसेमंद अंक दिलाते हैं, क्योंकि इनमें याद करने से ज़्यादा **प्रारूप**, **विषय-वस्तु** और **भाषा** का ध्यान रखना होता है।

| आधार | परीक्षक क्या देखते हैं |
|---|---|
| प्रारूप | पता, दिनांक, विषय, संबोधन, समापन |
| विषय-वस्तु | पूछे गए सभी बिंदु, क्रम |
| भाषा | शुद्ध वर्तनी, विराम चिह्न, शब्द-सीमा |

**तीन मिनट की योजना:** प्रश्न दो बार पढ़ें; *कौन लिख रहा है, किसे, किस विषय पर, कितने शब्दों में* — रेखांकित करें; चार–पाँच बिंदु लिखें; फिर लिखना शुरू करें।

check.q: लेखन-प्रश्न में सबसे पहले क्या करना चाहिए?
options: प्रश्न ध्यान से पढ़कर बिंदु बनाना
check.why: प्रश्न पढ़कर बिंदु बनाने से उत्तर क्रमबद्ध और पूरा बनता है।

sections.md:
प्रधानाचार्य, संपादक, अधिकारी आदि को।

**प्रारूप:**
1. सेवा में, पद, पता
2. दिनांक
3. विषय
4. संबोधन — *महोदय/महोदया*
5. विषय-वस्तु — पहला अनुच्छेद: उद्देश्य; दूसरा: विवरण; तीसरा: निवेदन
6. समापन — *भवदीय/भवदीया* या *आपका आज्ञाकारी शिष्य*
7. नाम, कक्षा/पता

**आदर्श नमूना (प्रधानाचार्य को अवकाश हेतु):**
> सेवा में, प्रधानाचार्य, केंद्रीय विद्यालय, लखनऊ
> दिनांक: 27 नवंबर 2026
> विषय: दो दिन के अवकाश हेतु प्रार्थना-पत्र
> महोदय, सविनय निवेदन है कि मुझे कल रात से तेज़ बुखार है। डॉक्टर ने दो दिन आराम की सलाह दी है। अतः कृपया मुझे 27 और 28 नवंबर का अवकाश देने की कृपा करें।
> आपका आज्ञाकारी शिष्य, अमन वर्मा, कक्षा 8-ब

मित्र, माता-पिता, संबंधियों को।

**प्रारूप:** पता, दिनांक, संबोधन (*प्रिय मित्र राहुल / पूज्य पिताजी*), अभिवादन (*सप्रेम नमस्ते / सादर चरण-स्पर्श*), विषय-वस्तु, समापन (*तुम्हारा मित्र / आपका प्रिय पुत्र*), नाम।

**ध्यान दें:** विषय-पंक्ति नहीं लिखी जाती। भाषा आत्मीय हो, पर शुद्ध हो।

**उदाहरण विषय:** छोटे भाई को मोबाइल का सीमित प्रयोग करने की सलाह; मित्र को जन्मदिन की बधाई; दादी को गाँव की याद।

check.q: पिताजी को पत्र में समापन क्या होगा?
check.why: अनौपचारिक पत्र में संबंध के अनुसार 'आपका प्रिय पुत्र' जैसा समापन होता है।

sections.md:
**रूपरेखा:** 1. भूमिका (रोचक आरंभ, सूक्ति या प्रश्न) 2. मुख्य भाग — 3–4 उपशीर्षक 3. उपसंहार (सुझाव, निष्कर्ष)।

**उदाहरण — 'वर्षा ऋतु':**
- *भूमिका:* जेठ की तपन के बाद आकाश में काले बादल जैसे वरदान बनकर आते हैं।
- *आगमन और दृश्य:* मिट्टी की सोंधी गंध, मोर का नाच, खेतों में हरियाली।
- *लाभ:* फ़सल, जल-भंडार, गर्मी से राहत।
- *हानियाँ:* बाढ़, कीचड़, मच्छर और रोग।
- *उपसंहार:* वर्षा जल का संचय करें।

**अन्य विषय:** मेरा प्रिय त्योहार, पर्यावरण प्रदूषण, विज्ञान के चमत्कार, डिजिटल भारत, समय का सदुपयोग, पुस्तकालय का महत्व।

**सूचना (लगभग 50 शब्द, बॉक्स में):** संस्था का नाम → 'सूचना' → दिनांक → शीर्षक → क्या, कब, कहाँ, कौन, किससे संपर्क → नाम, पद।

**संदेश (बॉक्स में):** दिनांक, समय, संबोधन, संदेश, नाम। जैसे — *माँ, मौसी जी का फ़ोन आया था। वे शाम सात बजे की ट्रेन से आ रही हैं। स्टेशन पर लेने जाना है। — रिया*

**विज्ञापन (25–50 शब्द):** आकर्षक शीर्षक, उत्पाद/सेवा का नाम, विशेषताएँ, छूट, संपर्क-सूत्र, नारा। जैसे — *'पढ़ो इंडिया पुस्तक मेला' — 1–7 दिसंबर, गांधी मैदान, पटना — सभी पुस्तकों पर 20% छूट!*

check.q: सूचना में कौन-सी चीज़ अनिवार्य है?
options: दिनांक, शीर्षक और जारी करने वाले का नाम-पद
check.why: सूचना में दिनांक, शीर्षक, विवरण और जारीकर्ता का नाम-पद अनिवार्य हैं।

sections.md:
**संवाद:** पात्रों के नाम के बाद कोलन (:) लगाकर बोलचाल की स्वाभाविक भाषा में बातचीत। भाव कोष्ठक में लिख सकते हैं। 6–10 संवाद।

*उदाहरण (दुकानदार–ग्राहक):*
ग्राहक: भैया, यह कॉपी कितने की है?
दुकानदार: चालीस रुपये की।
ग्राहक: थोड़ा कम कीजिए, दस ले रहा हूँ।
दुकानदार: (मुस्कुराकर) ठीक है, पैंतीस लगा दूँगा।

**कहानी लेखन:** दी गई रूपरेखा पर शीर्षक दें; आरंभ–समस्या–चरम–समाधान–सीख का क्रम रखें; भूतकाल का प्रयोग; अंत में सीख।

अपठित = जो पहले न पढ़ा हो। गद्यांश पढ़कर प्रश्नों के उत्तर, शीर्षक, शब्दार्थ, व्याकरण पूछे जाते हैं।

**विधि:**
1. गद्यांश एक बार पूरा पढ़ें; मुख्य भाव समझें।
2. प्रश्न पढ़ें, फिर गद्यांश में उत्तर वाली पंक्ति खोजें।
3. उत्तर अपने शब्दों में, पूरे वाक्य में लिखें।
4. **शीर्षक** — छोटा, सारगर्भित, केंद्रीय भाव वाला।

**अभ्यास गद्यांश (मौलिक):**
> पेड़ धरती के फेफड़े हैं। वे हमें प्राणवायु देते हैं, वर्षा लाने में सहायता करते हैं और मिट्टी को बहने से रोकते हैं। फिर भी शहर बढ़ाने के लिए हम उन्हें बेरहमी से काट रहे हैं। यदि हर विद्यार्थी अपने जन्मदिन पर एक पौधा लगाए और उसकी देखभाल करे, तो कुछ ही वर्षों में हमारे नगर फिर हरे-भरे हो सकते हैं।

प्रश्न: (क) पेड़ों को धरती के फेफड़े क्यों कहा गया है? (ख) लेखक विद्यार्थियों को क्या सुझाव देता है? (ग) उचित शीर्षक दीजिए। (घ) 'हरा-भरा' में कौन-सा समास है?

check.q: ऊपर के गद्यांश का सबसे उचित शीर्षक क्या होगा?
check.why: पूरा गद्यांश पेड़ों के महत्व और संरक्षण पर केंद्रित है।

sections.md:
कविता के अंश पर प्रश्न: भाव, शब्दार्थ, अलंकार, शीर्षक।

**विधि:** पहले भाव समझें — कवि क्या कह रहा है, किस भावना से (प्रेरणा, प्रकृति-प्रेम, देश-प्रेम)। फिर प्रश्न। उत्तर में कविता की पंक्ति जस-की-तस न उतारें, भाव अपने शब्दों में लिखें।

**अभ्यास पद्यांश (मौलिक):**
> चलो, नदी-सा बहते जाएँ,
> पत्थर आए, राह बनाएँ।
> थककर भी जो रुक न पाए,
> वही किनारे फूल खिलाए।

प्रश्न: (क) कवि किससे प्रेरणा लेने को कहता है? (ख) 'पत्थर' किसका प्रतीक है? (ग) 'नदी-सा बहते' में कौन-सा अलंकार है? (उपमा) (घ) उचित शीर्षक दीजिए।

**क्या आप जानते हैं?** 'सा, सी, से, सम, जैसा' आदि वाचक शब्द दिखें तो प्रायः **उपमा अलंकार** होता है।

summary: लेखन में प्रारूप, विषय-वस्तु और भाषा पर अंक मिलते हैं।
औपचारिक पत्र: सेवा में, दिनांक, विषय, महोदय, भवदीय।
अनौपचारिक पत्र में विषय-पंक्ति नहीं होती।
निबंध: भूमिका, उपशीर्षकों में मुख्य भाग, उपसंहार।
सूचना और संदेश बॉक्स में लिखे जाते हैं।
विज्ञापन: शीर्षक, विशेषताएँ, छूट, संपर्क, नारा।
संवाद स्वाभाविक बोलचाल की भाषा में हों।
कहानी: आरंभ, समस्या, चरम, समाधान, सीख।
अपठित गद्यांश: पढ़ें, खोजें, अपने शब्दों में उत्तर दें।
अपठित पद्यांश: भाव, प्रतीक और अलंकार पहचानें।
practice: नगर निगम अधिकारी को अपने मोहल्ले की सफ़ाई हेतु पत्र लिखिए।
छोटे भाई को सुबह जल्दी उठने की सलाह देते हुए पत्र लिखिए।
'मेरा प्रिय खेल' पर 200 शब्दों में निबंध लिखिए।
विद्यालय में वृक्षारोपण कार्यक्रम की सूचना लिखिए।
एक नए पेन का विज्ञापन तैयार कीजिए।
डॉक्टर और रोगी के बीच संवाद लिखिए।
'ईमानदारी का फल' विषय पर एक कहानी लिखिए।
ऊपर दिए गद्यांश के सभी प्रश्नों के उत्तर लिखिए।
ऊपर दिए पद्यांश का भावार्थ अपने शब्दों में लिखिए।

rd-school-c8-hindi.vyakaran.title: हिंदी व्याकरण (कक्षा 8) — संपूर्ण साथी
rd-school-c8-hindi.vyakaran.subtitle: वर्ण से वाक्य तक: संधि, समास, उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय, कारक, काल, वाच्य, अलंकार और मुहावरे

sections.md:
जैसे किसी नए शहर में नक्शा रास्ता दिखाता है, वैसे ही व्याकरण भाषा को शुद्ध बोलने-लिखने का रास्ता दिखाता है। इस साथी में कक्षा 8 के सभी व्याकरण-बिंदु क्रम से हैं: **वर्ण-विचार, शब्द-भेद, संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण, क्रिया, काल, वाच्य, कारक, संधि, समास, उपसर्ग-प्रत्यय, पर्यायवाची-विलोम, अनेकार्थी शब्द, वाक्य-भेद, अलंकार, मुहावरे-लोकोक्तियाँ और वर्तनी-शुद्धि।**

**वर्ण:** भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि। हिंदी में **स्वर** (अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ) और **व्यंजन** (क से ह तक, साथ में क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र संयुक्त व्यंजन) होते हैं। अनुस्वार (ं) और विसर्ग (ः) भी हैं; चंद्रबिंदु (ँ) अनुनासिक ध्वनि बताता है।

check.q: 'ज्ञ' किस प्रकार का वर्ण है?
check.why: ज्ञ = ज् + ञ, इसलिए यह संयुक्त व्यंजन है।

sections.md:
**संज्ञा** — नाम। भेद: व्यक्तिवाचक (गंगा, दिल्ली), जातिवाचक (नदी, शहर), भाववाचक (मिठास, बचपन)। भाववाचक बनाना: *मीठा → मिठास, बच्चा → बचपन, अपना → अपनापन, लड़का → लड़कपन, चढ़ना → चढ़ाई।*

**सर्वनाम** — संज्ञा के स्थान पर। भेद: पुरुषवाचक (मैं, तुम, वह), निश्चयवाचक (यह, वह), अनिश्चयवाचक (कोई, कुछ), संबंधवाचक (जो–सो), प्रश्नवाचक (कौन, क्या), निजवाचक (आप, स्वयं)।

**विशेषण** — संज्ञा/सर्वनाम की विशेषता। भेद: गुणवाचक (लाल, ईमानदार), संख्यावाचक (पाँच, कुछ), परिमाणवाचक (दो लीटर, थोड़ा), सार्वनामिक (यह किताब)। जिसकी विशेषता बताई जाए, वह **विशेष्य**।

**क्रिया** — काम का होना या करना। सकर्मक (कर्म हो: *राम फल खाता है*), अकर्मक (कर्म न हो: *बच्चा सोता है*)। प्रेरणार्थक: *पढ़ना → पढ़ाना → पढ़वाना।*

**काल** — क्रिया का समय।

| काल | उदाहरण |
|---|---|
| वर्तमान | मीरा गाती है / गा रही है |
| भूत | मीरा ने गाया / गा रही थी / गा चुकी थी |
| भविष्य | मीरा गाएगी / गा रही होगी |

**वाच्य** — कर्ता, कर्म या भाव में से किसकी प्रधानता है।
- **कर्तृवाच्य:** *सीता पत्र लिखती है।*
- **कर्मवाच्य:** *सीता द्वारा पत्र लिखा जाता है।* (कर्ता के साथ 'द्वारा/से')
- **भाववाच्य:** *मुझसे चला नहीं जाता।* (अकर्मक क्रिया, प्रायः असमर्थता)

check.q: 'बच्चों द्वारा गीत गाया गया' — कौन-सा वाच्य है?
check.why: कर्ता के साथ 'द्वारा' और कर्म (गीत) प्रधान है, इसलिए कर्मवाच्य।

sections.md:
संज्ञा/सर्वनाम का क्रिया से संबंध बताने वाले चिह्न।

| कारक | चिह्न | उदाहरण |
|---|---|---|
| कर्ता | ने | राम ने पढ़ा |
| कर्म | को | मोहन को बुलाओ |
| करण | से, के द्वारा | कलम से लिखो |
| संप्रदान | को, के लिए | गरीबों के लिए दान |
| अपादान | से (अलग होना) | पेड़ से पत्ता गिरा |
| संबंध | का, के, की | राम की किताब |
| अधिकरण | में, पर | मेज़ पर पुस्तक |
| संबोधन | हे, अरे | अरे बच्चो! |

**ध्यान दें:** करण और अपादान दोनों में 'से' है — करण में साधन, अपादान में अलगाव।

दो ध्वनियों के मेल से होने वाला परिवर्तन।

**स्वर संधि**
- दीर्घ: *विद्या + आलय = विद्यालय* (आ + आ = आ)
- गुण: *महा + इंद्र = महेंद्र* (आ + इ = ए); *सूर्य + उदय = सूर्योदय* (अ + उ = ओ)
- वृद्धि: *सदा + एव = सदैव* (आ + ए = ऐ)
- यण: *इति + आदि = इत्यादि* (इ + आ = या)
- अयादि: *ने + अन = नयन*

**व्यंजन संधि:** *जगत् + ईश = जगदीश, सत् + जन = सज्जन, उत् + लास = उल्लास।*

**विसर्ग संधि:** *नमः + ते = नमस्ते, निः + चल = निश्चल, मनः + योग = मनोयोग।*

check.q: 'सूर्योदय' का संधि-विच्छेद क्या है?
check.why: अ + उ = ओ (गुण संधि), इसलिए सूर्य + उदय।

sections.md:
दो या अधिक शब्दों को मिलाकर नया छोटा शब्द बनाना; उसे अलग करना **समास-विग्रह**।

| समास | पहचान | उदाहरण → विग्रह |
|---|---|---|
| अव्ययीभाव | पहला पद अव्यय | यथाशक्ति → शक्ति के अनुसार; प्रतिदिन → हर दिन |
| तत्पुरुष | कारक चिह्न लुप्त | राजपुत्र → राजा का पुत्र; रसोईघर → रसोई के लिए घर |
| कर्मधारय | विशेषण–विशेष्य/उपमा | नीलकमल → नीला है जो कमल; चंद्रमुख → चंद्र के समान मुख |
| द्विगु | पहला पद संख्या | त्रिभुज → तीन भुजाओं का समूह; चौराहा |
| द्वंद्व | दोनों पद प्रधान, 'और' | माता-पिता → माता और पिता; दाल-रोटी |
| बहुव्रीहि | अन्य अर्थ प्रधान | लंबोदर → लंबा है उदर जिसका अर्थात् गणेश; दशानन → रावण |

**क्या आप जानते हैं?** 'नीलकंठ' कर्मधारय भी हो सकता है (नीला कंठ) और बहुव्रीहि भी (नीला है कंठ जिसका — शिव)। अर्थ से भेद तय होता है।

check.q: 'माता-पिता' में कौन-सा समास है?
check.why: दोनों पद प्रधान हैं और 'और' से जुड़ते हैं, इसलिए द्वंद्व।

sections.md:
**उपसर्ग** — शब्द के आगे जुड़कर अर्थ बदलें: *अ* (अज्ञान), *अन* (अनपढ़), *प्र* (प्रगति), *वि* (विदेश), *सु* (सुपुत्र), *दुर्/दुस्* (दुर्गुण, दुस्साहस), *निर्/निस्* (निर्दोष, निश्चिंत), *उप* (उपवन), *पुनर्* (पुनर्जन्म)।

**प्रत्यय** — शब्द के पीछे: *-आई* (पढ़ाई), *-इक* (धार्मिक), *-ता* (सुंदरता), *-पन* (बचपन), *-वाला* (दूधवाला), *-ईय* (भारतीय), *-आवट* (सजावट)।

**पर्यायवाची:** पानी — जल, नीर, वारि; सूर्य — रवि, दिनकर, भानु; पेड़ — वृक्ष, तरु, विटप।
**विलोम:** आदर–अनादर, उदय–अस्त, सजीव–निर्जीव, आयात–निर्यात।
**अनेकार्थी:** *कर* — हाथ, टैक्स, किरण; *अंबर* — आकाश, वस्त्र; *हार* — माला, पराजय।
**अनेक शब्दों के लिए एक शब्द:** जो ईश्वर में विश्वास रखे — आस्तिक; जिसका कोई शत्रु न हो — अजातशत्रु; जो दिखाई न दे — अदृश्य।

**वाक्य-भेद (रचना):** सरल (*वह घर गया*), संयुक्त (*वह घर गया और सो गया*), मिश्र (*जब वह घर गया, तब वर्षा हो रही थी*)। **अर्थ के आधार पर:** विधानवाचक, निषेधवाचक, प्रश्नवाचक, आज्ञावाचक, इच्छावाचक, संदेहवाचक, विस्मयादिवाचक, संकेतवाचक।

**अलंकार:**
- अनुप्रास — एक वर्ण की आवृत्ति: *चारु चंद्र की चंचल किरणें*
- यमक — एक शब्द, अलग अर्थ: *कनक कनक ते सौ गुनी* (सोना/धतूरा)
- श्लेष — एक शब्द में कई अर्थ चिपके हों
- उपमा — 'सा, सी, समान': *मुख चंद्रमा-सा सुंदर*
- रूपक — उपमेय पर उपमान का आरोप: *चरण-कमल*
- उत्प्रेक्षा — 'मानो, जनु': *मानो झूम रहे हों तरु*

**मुहावरे:** *आँखों का तारा* (बहुत प्यारा), *नौ दो ग्यारह होना* (भाग जाना), *दाँतों तले उँगली दबाना* (चकित होना), *ईद का चाँद होना* (बहुत दिनों बाद दिखना)। **लोकोक्ति:** *अधजल गगरी छलकत जाय* — कम ज्ञानी अधिक दिखावा करता है।

**वर्तनी-शुद्धि:** आशीर्वाद (न कि आर्शीवाद), उज्ज्वल, कवयित्री, प्रदर्शनी, सम्मान, परीक्षा, श्रीमती।

check.q: 'चरण-कमल' में कौन-सा अलंकार है?
check.why: चरणों को ही कमल मान लिया गया है — उपमेय पर उपमान का आरोप, अतः रूपक।

workedExamples.q: 'राष्ट्रपति' का समास-विग्रह और भेद बताइए।
कर्मवाच्य में बदलिए: माली पौधे सींचता है।
workedExamples.answer: माली द्वारा पौधे सींचे जाते हैं।

workedExamples.q: 'निश्चल' का संधि-विच्छेद कीजिए।
मिश्र वाक्य बनाइए: परिश्रमी छात्र सफल होता है।
workedExamples.answer: जो छात्र परिश्रम करता है, वह सफल होता है।

summary: वर्ण: स्वर और व्यंजन; अनुस्वार, विसर्ग, चंद्रबिंदु।
संज्ञा के तीन भेद; भाववाचक संज्ञा बनाना सीखें।
सर्वनाम के छह भेद; विशेषण के चार भेद।
क्रिया: सकर्मक, अकर्मक, प्रेरणार्थक।
तीन काल; तीन वाच्य।
आठ कारक — करण और अपादान में अंतर।
संधि: स्वर, व्यंजन, विसर्ग।
समास के छह भेद और विग्रह।
उपसर्ग आगे, प्रत्यय पीछे जुड़ते हैं।
वाक्य: सरल, संयुक्त, मिश्र।
अलंकार: अनुप्रास, यमक, श्लेष, उपमा, रूपक, उत्प्रेक्षा।
मुहावरे वाक्यांश हैं; लोकोक्ति पूर्ण कथन।
practice: भाववाचक संज्ञा बनाइए: मित्र, सुंदर, गिरना, मनुष्य।
संधि-विच्छेद कीजिए: महेंद्र, सदैव, इत्यादि, जगदीश।
समास-विग्रह कर भेद लिखिए: यथाशक्ति, चौराहा, दशानन, नीलकमल।
कारक पहचानिए: बच्चा छत से गिरा।
भाववाच्य में बदलिए: मैं नहीं सो सकता।
उपसर्ग और मूल शब्द अलग कीजिए: प्रगति, दुर्गुण, निर्दोष।
दो-दो पर्यायवाची लिखिए: सूर्य, पानी, कमल।
अलंकार पहचानिए: पीपर पात सरिस मन डोला।
मुहावरों से वाक्य बनाइए: नौ दो ग्यारह होना, आँखों का तारा।
शुद्ध कीजिए: आर्शीवाद, उज्वल, परिक्षा।
